title: Account Management
content:
If a hub doesn't have a explicit policy on account management such as login failures, the defaults will be as follows.  Note that NCIPhub has explicitly set such policies (see the hub-specific information for NCIPhub).  Account management policies can be applied by following the account management procedures.

SSH Key Management Policies

See this sub-page

Password Reset Frequency

Password resets will be rate limited to 2/hour per user.

Login Failures and Bans

By default, password login attempts will be rate limited to 10 in 2 hours, per user, with a ban of up to 2 hours.  The mechanism used by the CMS counts the number of failures over the number of hours specified and blocks logins until the oldest failure falls outside that window.  So if the oldest failure was nearly two hours ago, then it could be possible for someone to be banned only for a few minutes.  Although 50 in 5 hours and 10 in 1 hour is the same rate, the implementation is such that the former can result in a ban of 5 hours and the latter, a ban of 1 hour maximum. 

If an IP address is abused to attack many accounts, that address will get banned by engaging the "fail2ban" mechanism, which must be turned on.  If 5 accounts/hour get banned from the same IP address, then that IP address will be blocked by calling fail2ban. 

The procedure for the implementation of this policy is in the administrative section, "Account Management"

Login Failures and Bans -- Desired Future Policy

By default, password login attempts for (IP address, user) pairs will be rate limited to 10/hour.  If an IP address is abused to attack many accounts, many (IP address, user) pairs will get banned by engaging the "fail2ban" mechanism, which must be turned on.  If 10 pairs/hour get banned then the IP address will be blocked by calling fail2ban.  If a user account gets attacked from many different IP addresses, the account must get locked to protect against distributed attacks.

Password Strength

NIH FISMA Requirements

  • Password length must be at least eight (8) characters in length.
  • Passwords are required to be a combination of at least one (1) character from each of the four (4) character categories:
    • Capital letters (A‐Z),
    • Lower case letters (a‐z),
    • Numeric characters (0‐9), and
    • Special characters (e.g., !@#$%^&*()_+|~‐=\`{}[]:";'<>?,./).
    • Maximum Password Age/Change frequency: Must be changed at least every one hundred twenty (120) days.
  • New password must be different from the previous six (6) generations of passwords.  This can be satisfied by requiring passwords to be different from the passwords used in the preceeding 6*120 = 720 days.

General HIPAA Requirements

Hubs needing regulatory compliance or having other security concerns, the following additional characteristics must be mandated:

    Must contain more than 4 unique characters
    Must not contain your name or parts of your name
    Must not contain your username
    Must be different than the previous password (re-use of the same password will not be allowed for one (1) year)
    Passwords must be changed every N days, where N is a year or less.

Regular Requirements

For hubs without special security requirements, passwords must at a minimum have the following characteristics (CMS administrative interface path Users -> Members -> Passwords):

    Must contain at least 1 letter
    Must contain at least 1 number or punctuation mark
    Must be at least 8 characters long
    Passwords must be changed every N days, where N is 5 years or less.

Password Hashes

The password hashing mechanism must use SHA512.

title: SSH Key Management Policies
content:
SSH is central and crucial to the administration of our systems. It is important that SSH communications be secure.

Passphrases

This is a requirement.  SSH private keys, except those used for scripting and automated tasks, must have a passphrase set for protection.  It is OK to store the passphrase in a password store mechanism that is unlocked when you login on your workstation, and automatically provides the passphrase when needed.  The passphrase must have a strength comparable or greater than that of a help.hubzero.org password (see password policy).  There are no requirements to change the passphrase periodically;  instead the SSH key pair is expected to be changed (see key lifetime below).  Changing the passphrase wouldn't protect accounts whose private key has been compromised, and wouldn't prevent cracking the passphrase of a private key that was copied.

Key Strength and Lifetime vs Risk

This is a requirement. 

Overview

Use 2048-bit or 3072-bit RSA keys, or the equivalent listed below if using another algorithm than RSA.  Shorter keys must be replaced immediately.  SSH key pairs should be replaced at every opportunity instead of copying key pairs, e.g., when upgrading systems.  See the "One key pair per origin" suggestion below.  Ciphersuites that are currently considered secure should be explicitly selected, and others disabled.  Privileged users must avoid storing private keys on networked filesystems.

Reasoning

The following attempts to balance the administrative power given to accounts versus how the SSH keys are managed.

1. Key Length and Cryptoperiod SSH keys can be compromised through brute force if they are small, or can be exposed at some point in time through a host compromise or mishandling. The maximum duration for the use of an SSH key pair is called a cryptoperiod, and attempts to minimize the risk of unknowingly using a compromised key pair.

For RSA key pairs:

  • 1024 bit keys are too weak and are unacceptable for use at HUBzero for administrative purposes or for privileged users (e.g., access-* group members). Unprivileged users may use those if they wish.
  • 2048 bit keys will have a cryptoperiod of 3 years.
  • 3072-bit keys or more will have a cryptoperiod of 10 years.
  • All keys must be changed at least every 10 years, and in the case of system accounts used for backups or configuration management, the keys must be changed every time a user who had access to the private key leaves HUBzero.
b=3072; ssh-keygen -t rsa -b $b -C "created `date +'%Y-%m-%d'` with $b bits"


For ed25519 key pairs:

  • All keys must be changed at least every 10 years, and in the case of system accounts used for backups or configuration management, the keys must be changed every time a user who had access to the private key leaves HUBzero.
ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "created `date +'%Y-%m-%d'`"

For ECDSA key pairs:

  • 256-bit keys will have a cryptoperiod of 3 years.
  • 384-bit keys or more will have a cryptoperiod of 10 years.
  • All keys must be changed at least every 10 years, and in the case of system accounts used for backups or configuration management, the keys must be changed every time a user who had access to the private key leaves HUBzero.
ssh-keygen -t ecdsa -C "created `date +'%Y-%m-%d'`"

For DSA key pairs:

  • DSA keys are too weak and are unacceptable for use at HUBzero for administrative purposes or for privileged users (e.g., access-* group members). Unprivileged users may use those if they wish but should note that those keys are unsupported starting with OpenSSH 7.0

To facilitate the implementation of this policy, a creation date or expiration date should be appended to the comment section of SSH keys (at the end, after “==”). The commands above use the “C” option to create a comment with the date.

The number of bits for existing keys can be found with this command:

ssh-keygen -l -f  path

2. Ciphersuites

The recommended algorithms for use at HUBzero are:

  • MACs hmac-sha2-512,hmac-sha2-256,hmac-sha1
  • KexAlgorithms diffie-hellman-group-exchange-sha256,ecdh-sha2-nistp256
  • Ciphers aes256-ctr,aes192-ctr,aes128-ctr

However exceptions are made for compatibility with MySQL Workbench. The MAC “hmac-sha1” is required for MySQL Workbench (catalyzecare see ticket #514).

3. Sudoers

People with sudo privileges aren’t allowed to login using passwords and must use SSH keys.

4. NFS

On hubs using NFS for home directories, the authorized_keys file must be moved off NFS onto local media such as at /var/homes/username/.ssh

5. SSH Version

HUBzero systems should use OpenSSH version 1:6.6p1-4~bpo70+1 or later.

6. Host keys

Host keys must not be copied when moving to different hardware; new host keys must be generated instead. For VMs, host keys are subject to the above policies.

7. Rsync backup service keys

Each backup server using rsync shall have its own SSH key pair.

Remove Public SSH keys Promptly

This is a requirement.  Whenever a private key is lost, exposed, or at the end of its recommended cryptoperiod, or when a staff member's account is closed or terminated or when the access is not needed anymore, the matching public keys MUST be removed from all authorized_keys files.

One key pair per origin

This is a suggestion.  SSH key pairs should not be used forever.  To make it easier to expire SSH keys, avoid copying SSH private keys around, even if they are protected by a passphrase. Instead, consider the private key bound to a particular machine. Whenever you upgrade a machine, or decommission one, remove the corresponding public key in authorized_keys files.  For example, create a key pair on a laptop and a different one on a desktop. Then if the laptop is lost, it’s easy to remove the corresponding public key from servers, without removing all your access.

title: Database Accounts Policy
content:
Host Wildcards

The use of wildcards to specify the allowed sources of connections is strongly discouraged (e.g., in the mysql.user.host column). The main CMS account MUST NOT allow host wildcards for any reason, as this account is authoritative for almost all user accounts, group membership and authentication.

Remote Access to Database Accounts

Direct remote access to a MySQL account requires SSL to protect the connection, unless the account provides only read access to public data.  The MySQL account is protected by setting mysql.user.ssl_type to a value like “ANY”. 

MySQL Accounts for people

User grants to a hub's database MUST NOT allow access to the password hashes of other users unless required, and even then it must be approved by the HUBzero ISO.

Views

Use “SQL SECURITY INVOKER” instead of “SQL SECURITY DEFINER” in view creation statements. Otherwise, views need to be dropped and recreated when changing user access permissions. With SQL SECURITY DEFINER, you will get a warning/error if the combo user@host does not exist, every time you access the view.

title: Configuration Management System Requirements
content:
• All hosts must have the configuration of their operating system and services managed by a configuration management system (e.g., Ogre, Puppet, Ansible).
  • The configuration management system should be run periodically to detect deviations, alert, and rectify them
  • The configuration management system must manage the configuration of all services which are subject to an SLA
  • The configuration management system should manage the configuration of all services that are common to (i.e., installed on) more than one host
  • The configuration management system must be able to restore accurately a service's configuration when operating on a fresh package install
  • On non-production systems, the periodic run can be disabled temporarily for debugging or development purposes, to test different configurations.

title: Data Depot Considerations
content:
Things to consider when a hub wants to use Data Depot for storage

  • Backups are not included, but snapshots are.  They don't offer the full protection of backups vs disasters or the Data Depot system failing or being fully compromised, and they don't go back as far as HUBzero backups do, but they significantly reduce risks, are convenient, useful, and offer the capability of recovering past versions of files.
  • A proxy account must be setup, which must own all files on Data Depot.  This works well if the owner of all storage is www-data on the hub, so it works for projects (See PURR) and in some special configurations, for subdirectories of components (see smarteragriculture.org).  In this configuration only a single user (e.g., www-data) can access the files.
  • A proxy account acting on behalf of many other users is less secure because it requires the use of the "allow_others" mount option.  Furthermore, access must be setup with either the use of bindfs or a tangle of bind mounts (one for each user).  It requires scripts to regenerate the mounts on demand, or the bindfs utility which isn't available and supported on old kernels.  See Diagrid.
  • Using Data Depot for component storage, and mounting it under the Apache Document Root, is risky if PHP execution isn't disabled inside the mount.  Rogue PHP scripts written on Data Depot could run on the hub, and compromise the hub.  Thankfully this isn't difficult, but may limit what can be done.  See Smarteragriculturehub.
  • When getting storage for what RCAC calls a "lab", certain directory structure and group permissions are in place.  Hub mounts should be placed in Data Depot's "data" directory and secured by minimizing membership in the "hubname-data" group.  Only that group can read or write what is put there:

    drwxrws---+   5 root purr-data    512 Sep 27 12:11 data

    The other directories have more open permissions.  As SMB access is public to Purdue, does not require 2-factor authentication and is only a password that can be exposed by weak authentication mechanisms, everyone who has a career account and is in the (hubname)-data group could act as a conduit for attackers to read or modify projects.  Risk is lowered by removing people from the (hubname)-data group.  The dedicated account for connecting to Data Depot should be the only one that can.

Password

Regardless of the access method used, password access is always enabled.  I recommend that hubs using Data Depot commit to changing the service account password frequently.  Hub owners should be aware of this when considering the use of Data Depot.  There is no way to programmatically regularly change the password of the account used to connect, one must use the Purdue Career Account password change web page.

Choice of Connection Method

Data Depot accounts have a huge attack surface:  Globus, SSH, SMB, etc.  These access methods are always enabled, except for NFS.  There is currently no way to request that the unused methods be disabled.  For hubs, we considered SMB, SSH (SSHFS), and NFS. 

SMB

  • SMB access cannot be restricted by IP address, only by password.  This is an administrative restriction, SMB allows both simultaneously, but the Data Depot administrators aren't setup to support this.
  • SMB access doesn't offer SMB3 security features such as encryption.  Only very recent Linux kernels support this.
  • SMB access allows old authentication mechanisms (sec=ntlm) so the account can be compromised more easily.
  • SMB access has problems with special characters, even when using the "mapchars" option.  PURR had these errors when testing SMB:
    • "Invalid argument (22)" with filenames including an escaped return (backslash n)
    • "No such file or directory" with a filename including quotes and a question mark
  • SMB gave "Operation not supported" errors with symlinks when copying projects
  • SMB shares can't be mounted from within OpenVZ containers.  They must be mounted on the OpenVZ host.  There, everything appears owned by the proxy user (www-data, id 33) because of the mount options selected. A bind mount makes it available inside containers. 

NFS

  • NFS is available only by special request.
  • NFS on Data Depot is only v3, there is no way to have encryption. 
  • NFSv3 can only offer IP address restriction, without passwords.
  • NFS exposes the entire account storage.  It is not possible to select a subdirectory for export.  For example, all of /depot/purr is exposed, instead of only /depot/purr/data.  This is related to the use of GPFS
  • The NFS mount point must be mounted inside a special protective directory.
    • Because the user on Data Depot has a different uid than our proxy user (www-data), NFS requires the use of the "all_squash" option on the server.  This makes the share world-writable and protected only by the IP address restriction. 
    • On the server, the share can be written to by any user.  The protective directory limits this access to only our proxy user (www-data).
    • SFTP access through the projfs fuse filesystem doesn't work with a symlink, it must use the protected mountpoint directly.  For example, on PURR the NFS mount is at /srv/protection/projects, with a symlink at /srv/projects pointing to it.  So projfs works with /srv/protection/projects, not /srv/projects.
    • Xymon monitoring requires that it be allowed to read the NFS mounts.  This is done by adding permissions to the protective directory, e.g., with "setfacl -m u:xymon:3 /export/protection"

SSHFS

  • SMB and NFS offer better availability and reliability than sshfs, because multiple physical servers can provide the service.  In their deployment, sshfs is less dependable because it is provided through a single virtual machine that uses NFS internally to connect to Data Depot.
  • Despite the above we have deployed sshfs and it has worked reliably.
  • SSHFS is the only way to provide an encrypted connection between the hub and Data Depot.  However, NFS is used between the VM providing SSHFS access and the actual Data Depot servers, so the security gain from encryption within a data center may be minimal, while introducing latency in file operations.
  • SFTP access through the projfs fuse filesystem doesn't work on top of an SSHFS mount, so this is inappropriate for hosting /srv/projects on Data Depot

title: Handling of SSL Certificates and Keys
content:
SSL private keys must be stored in as few locations as possible to minimize the risk of exposure and compromise.  Acceptable locations are:

  • On the host that needs to use the certificate
  • On the configuration management system that configures the host that needs that certificate (e.g., Ansible products or Ogre)
  • Temporarily in a specially designated secure location to facilitate transfer to one of the above 2, e.g., /opt/hubzero/HUB_SSL_Certs

Staff must be diligent in deleting SSL private keys from temporary storage, e.g., /opt/hubzero/HUB_SSL_Certs after deployment.  As a second line of defense, scripts will:

  • After 10 days (measured with ctime and mtime) directories in /opt/hubzero/HUB_SSL_Certs will be moved to a root-owned location (e.g., /root/old_SSL_certs)
  • After 10 more days in /root/old_SSL_certs they will be automatically deleted

At the final locations, the files should be accessible only by:

  • root
  • if needed, by the user under which the configuration management system operates
  • the system user that requires the SSL key to provide the relevant service.

title: Historical Policies
content: This section contains obsolete policies, kept for historical purposes (see subpages).

title: Staff Network Policy
content:
The staff network is wired ethernet, which is more difficult to attack than wireless.  Using the staff network grants privileged access past some HUBzero firewalls.  The staff network is divided into 3 address ranges:

  • DHCP service range.  This range offers automatic IP address assignment.  Because this is where unexpected devices will operate and we have no inventory of devices operating in this IP address range, and because hosts with automatically assigned IP addresses are difficult to locate, hosts in this range can't offer services to the internet.  This policy prevents incidents; for example we once had a computer on DHCP unexpectedly offering SSH service and it was compromised.  It was found only because it started spewing spam, otherwise it could have kept being used by attackers for a long time.  The SSH service was actually offered not by the OS, but by an embedded IPMI device in the machine, whose owner didn't know existed.  It was hard to track. 
  • Hosts with assigned hubzero.org names, whose owners want to offer SSH service to the internet.
  • Hosts with assigned hubzero.org names, whose owners do not want to offer SSH service to the internet. 

HUBzero will maintain a list of owners for all hosts with assigned hubzero.org names, to find, and get help from the owners should an incident happen.

Staff can request that the firewall be opened so their machines can offer services to Purdue or to the internet.  In that case, the enabled services MUST pass periodic network security scans.  Staff who self-manage these machines MUST secure them, including securing the configuration of the offered services and applying security patches, and MUST do due diligence in monitoring their machines for signs of compromise or unusual activity.

Network connections (PICs) to the staff network MUST NOT be offered outside offices and areas occupied by HUBzero staff.

title: Host Configuration Policy
content:
Logs

Logs are subject to the Purdue "IT Resource Logging (S-11)" standard.  Additionally we need to meet HIPAA criteria and FISMA certification requirements where appropriate. Logs are needed for audit capabilities.

Log Rotation

To support audit capabilities, hosts will be configured to keep one month's worth of logs.  As we keep 12 monthly backups, this provides 1 year's worth of logs.  Whether log rotation is daily, weekly or monthly depends on the size of the log and its function -- in some special cases logs are rotated based on log size.  Keeping large logs causes backup churn and is to be avoided.  Log rotation must be configured to use dates (e.g., example.log-2018-01-01) instead of appending a number (e.g., example.log.0) because the renaming due to the constant renumbering causes considerable wasteful churn in the backups.

Logging Controls

  • We use a remote logging server so even if an attacker erases the logs on a compromised servers, we have intact copies
  • A script verifies daily that all servers under configuration management are connected and reporting to the central logging server, and if any is missing, system administrators are alerted
  • Log auditing is done by removing known routine and benign events so that anything strange or unusual is brought to the attention of system administrators
  • /var/log on a separate logical volume to guarantee logs will have projected needed space even when a situation causes a lot of logging to happen
  • Logs are compressed when rotated to free space for more logging.  Size-based log rotation can be useful to preserve free space.

Email

Mail Transfer Agents (MTAs, e.g., Exim on Debian) must be configured to use TLS if they send mail outside the HUBzero or Purdue networks. The DMARC policy should be specified for all our domains, and MTAs should either have appropriate SPF records in DNS or be configured with DKIM.

Reserved Email Addresses

People expect to be able to contact us using some standard email contact addresses.  We should aim to conform to RFC 2142 which suggests public email addresses like the following:

  • info
  • marketing
  • sales
  • support
  • abuse
  • noc
  • security
  • postmaster
  • hostmaster
  • webmaster

Public-facing hosts, e.g., those whose names match domain names like hubzero.org, must at minimum be configured to accept email to:

  • abuse
  • security
  • hostmaster

Hubs must also provide email service for:

  • support

When to use aliases or mailing lists

Simple aliases are defined in /etc/aliases.  Aliases are fine for mail generated on the server itself, e.g., by daemons, cron jobs, events on a hub, or scripts.  However, mail received from the internet, e.g., to abuse, support, security and hostmaster can't be redirected immediately to staff addresses.  That's because it will seem like our server is sending mail on behalf of other companies (e.g., Google or Microsoft) so the messages may be dropped as spam depending on the DMARC policy of those companies and enforcement at the destination staff email server.  Mailing lists should be used to receive external mail.  

Aliases are very useful to funnel external mail to a mailing list hosted on the same server.  For example, on help.hubzero.org, hostmaster, webmaster, postmaster, security can all be aliases for the mailing list sysadmins@help.hubzero.org, provided the mailman configuration has those listed in the section "Recipient filters" in the box for "Alias names (regexps) which qualify as explicit to or cc destination names for this list."  Otherwise the messages will be held for moderation with the explanation that they have "implicit addresses".

DMARC, SPF and DKIM

These anti-spam measures allow remote or destination servers to verify that emails were sent legitimately.  Those that aren't legitimate (spam or phishing) can be quarantined or rejected and sent to us. This increases the reputation of our mail and protects our clients from some phishing attempts.  There are 2 methods to verify legitimacy: SPF and DKIM.  What to do with the mail is expressed by DMARC. 

SPF

Specifies the IP address of servers which are authorized to originate email.  This doesn't work well with mail forwarders, e.g., if your Purdue account is set to forward mail somewhere else.

DKIM

Cryptographically signs emails.  Receiving servers verify signatures by obtaining the public key from DNS records.  Most forwarders preserve the signature, so it works well for that.  DKIM requires that all sources of email sign emails, so it doesn't work well with servers that send automated emails and that don't have a mail transfer agent fully setup. 

HUBzero execution hosts or other infrastructure hosts typically aren't setup for DKIM.  They have the option of sending mail through a fully setup host which is then called a "smart host" (a.k.a. "relay host"), and the infrastructure hosts are then called "satellites".  However, this creates a single point of failure for sending mail.

DMARC

DMARC specifies how SPF and DKIM tests are to be handled and what to do if an email fails the tests (no action, quarantine or reject).  In general, if an email passes either SPF or DKIM, it is accepted.

title: a 1 ii A Risk Analysis
content:
HUBzero will take reasonable steps to identify and prioritize the risks to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of EPHI due to HUBzero software and its configuration.  However, the infrastructure provided by the Sherlock environment shall have its own separate risk analysis,  documented separately in the "SDSC Sherlock Risk Assessment Plan", not covered here.  For this purpose, the risk analysis will comprise:

-An inventory of which VMs are covered under HIPAA rules.

-An identification of potential threats to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of EPHI.

-An identification of weaknesses that may facilitate the realization of threats.

-An assessment of existing controls that mitigate the weaknesses.

-An assessment of the likelihood, impact, and overall risk posed by the weaknesses.

-Recommendations.


This analysis shall be updated every year. The results of the risk analysis shall be considered confidential. This means that it will only be shared with non-HUBzero staff on a need-to-know basis. Hard copies shall be kept in reasonably secure locations, and electronic copies shall not be available for public access.

Historical:  the risk analysis policy used at Purdue is in the old wiki.

title: a 1 ii (B) Risk Management
content:
1. Goal

HUBzero will implement security measures designed to reduce the risks to EPHI to a reasonable level, provided that applications making use of EPHI restrict themselves to an appropriately limited set of HUB features and infrastructure hosts, and communicate this set to HUBzero. Not all HUB functionality and all HUB hosts can be secured to a level appropriate for handling EPHI information. HUBzero cannot alone provide a reasonable risk level for EPHI information without strong cooperation from HUB stakeholders and their considerable involvement in the risk management process.

2. Periodic Risk Management Process Requirements

a. Assessment and prioritization, on the basis of risks, of EPHI Systems.

b. Selection and implementation of reasonable, appropriate, and cost-effective security measures to manage, mitigate, or accept identified risks.

c. Security training and awareness on implemented security measures to relevant workforce members.

d. Periodic evaluation and revision, as necessary, of the security measures.

3. Risk management process

The risk management process for HUBzero systems, excluding the EPHI-handling applications, shall be conducted by HUBzero system administrators in consultation with the staff member most qualified with regards to security concerns, or by that staff member. The developers of applications handling EPHI information need to perform their own risk management, and be aware of the risks involved in their decision to enable and utilize available HUB functionality.

a. Risk analysis ­

The risk analysis required by HIPAA (see 164.308 a 1 ii (A)) is a sound basis for risk management activities. Ticket handling is also a good opportunity to discover risks. Non-trivial issues can be discussed on the “ncn-maint” mailing list if it might help resolve the following steps. HUBzero staff will be available for consultation by developers of applications handling EPHI information.

b. Risk prioritization ­

Risks identified in the risk analysis or otherwise shall be prioritized based on the overall calculated risk level. Amongst issues of equal level, potential impact to HUBzero systems where the existing controls are the weakest and the expected cost of remediation is the lowest shall be used for prioritization. Risks at the highest level should be handled as soon as possible. Responsibility for responding to discovered risks should be passed to an appropriate staff member, e.g., by filing a ticket. Non-confidential, non-urgent risks and their solution can be discussed using the HUBzero Wish system.

c. Method identification ­

The appropriate security methods to minimize or eliminate identified risks shall be identified. Security methods shall be identified based on the nature, feasibility, and effectiveness of the specific security method.

d. Cost-benefit analysis ­

HUBzero shall identify and define the costs and benefits of implementing or not implementing the identified security methods.

e. Security method selection ­

Based on the cost-benefit analysis, HUBzero shall select the most appropriate, reasonable, and cost-effective security methods for reducing the identified risks.

f. Assignment of responsibility ­

HUBzero staff with the appropriate expertise shall implement the selected security methods.

g. Security method implementation ­

The selected security methods shall be properly implemented by the responsible workforce members.

h. Security method evaluation ­

The selected and implemented security methods shall be evaluated and revised, as necessary, by the HUBzero staff member most qualified with regards to security concerns.

4. Strategies for Managing Risk

The strategies for managing risk shall be proportionate with the risks to and sensitivity of EPHI. The security measures shall reasonably protect the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of EPHI. The following methods are used to manage risk:

a. Situational Awareness

b. Risk acceptance­

c. Risk avoidance­

d. Risk limitation­

e. Risk transference­

4.1 Vulnerability Scanning

Vulnerability scanning is a strategy for situational awareness, and defined as control RA-5 in NIST SP 800-53. There are several types of vulnerability scans.  In the Sherlock environment, network vulnerability scanning, and scanning of the infrastructure, are handled by the Sherlock team.  HUBzero is responsible for "web application scanning" to detect vulnerabilities in the HUBzero software, and will do as follows:

a. Web application scans will be conducted monthly and when new vulnerabilities potentially affecting the system/applications are identified and reported;
b. The scans will identify findings by using the Common Vulnerability and Exposures (CVE) and the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS)
c. Vulnerability scan reports and results from security control assessments will be analyzed;
d. Legitimate vulnerabilities will be remediated in accordance with an NIH or IC risk assessment and per HHS and/or NIH policies
e. The information obtained from the vulnerability scanning process and security control assessments will be shared with the NIH CISO, NIH ISAO, NIH OSOP, and System Owner and IC CIO, ISSO, Privacy Coordinator, and System Owner

HUBzero will document the web application scanning process, with identified roles and responsibilities, incorporating appropriate federal oversight and separation of duties, in the "Procedures" section of the HUBzero documentation.

5. Results

The results of the risk management process shall be documented either in tickets, in the HUBzero wiki for the “production” group or in the software configuration management system’s (currently “Ansible”) comments and settings.

Historical: the risk management policy was documented in the old wiki.

title: a 1 ii (D) Information System Activity Review
content:
Goal

"Implement procedures to regularly review records of information system activity, such as audit logs, access reports, and security incident tracking reports."

Policy

The goal of this policy is to allow timely detection of problems and anomalies so that corrective actions can be taken before they create or become incidents, or to initiate incident response as appropriate.

HUBzero will develop and maintain procedures to review records of information system activity on a periodic basis.  This responsibility may be delegated to staff operating the environments where VMs are provisioned for HUBzero and in which they operate.  Additional reviews will be done as needed where incidents are reported or suspected, as defined in our Incident Response Plan. These procedures will use automated mechanisms to monitor logs and service statuses and extract relevant information, to generate alerts as appropriate.  Alerts will be directed to active duty and designated on-call personnel, of which there will always be at least one individual.  These individuals must keep their contact information up-to-date in the appropriate lists and system configurations, and maintain any required services.

System Activity Review Procedures

RDS Environment (not HIPAA-covered, not FISMA-certified):

Most of the system activity review is done by RDS staff, using their procedures and plans.  HUBzero also created a number of regularly run checks via the "cron" system, sending emails alerts to "sysadmins@hubzero.org".  In addition, the "PRTG" monitoring system will send emails to that list.  Every day, hubzero system administrators will:

  • Review emails sent to "sysadmins@hubzero.org" and take appropriate action, when necessary escalating issues to RDS staff by creating tickets by sending an email to "support@sdsc.edu" or communicating via "Slack".
  • Check the "PRTG Desktop" application status for our VMs, or review emails sent individually to system administrators with the subject "[SDSC Unified Monitor]"
  • Inform HUBzero management of any downtime incurred via the Slack channel "trouble" in the hubzero Slack workspace.

Sherlock Environment (HIPAA-covered):

Most of the system activity review is done by Sherlock staff, using their procedures and plans. Automated alerts that are in the scope of HUBzero responsibilities will be emailed to "sysadmins@hubzero.org".  HUBzero also created a number of regularly run checks via the "cron" system, sending emails alerts to "sysadmins@hubzero.org".  Every day, hubzero system administrators will:

  • Review emails sent to "sysadmins@hubzero.org" and take appropriate action, if necessary creating tickets by sending an email to "sherlocksupport@sdsc.edu" to request assistance from the Sherlock team.
  • Inform HUBzero management of any downtime incurred via the Slack channel "trouble" in the hubzero Slack workspace.
  • Managers pass this information along to designated contacts for each site operated by hubzero for anything of significant duration and importance.

Events to be reviewed at least weekly are defined by control AU-2:

  • Unsuccessful log-on attempts that result in a locked account/node (see table "jos_users_log_auth", status='blocked');
  • Configuration changes;
  • Application alerts and error messages;
  • System administration activities;
  • Modification of privileges and access; and
  • Account creation, modification, or deletion.

Purdue Environment (historical):

Every day:

  • Review system changes reported by rkhunter
  • Check if there are updates to apply to Debian systems
    • Login on control.hubzero.org
    • Run /root/bin/patch_pkgs to patch non-production systems and restart affected services
    • Run /root/bin/patch_production to patch production systems and restart affected services
  • Check if Xymon reported anything of importance.
  • Check if there were any backup errors
  • Read the "logcheck" automated emails, looking for anything warranting correction or response.
  • Check whether the installation of new kernel versions might have caused Yellow or Red alert for disk space on /boot. Remove extra, unneeded kernels that can consume all the space on /boot. See OS-specific procedures for suggested and example commands.

 

Related to:

NIST SP 800-53 control families "SI System and information integrity" and "AU Audit and Accountability":
(AU-1) Audit and Accountability Policy and Procedures
(AU-2) Auditable Events
(AU-3) Content of Audit Records
(AU-4) Audit Storage Capacity
(AU-5) Response to Audit Processing Failures
(AU-6) Audit Review, Analysis, and Reporting

 

Old wiki versions of this policy are at: https://help.hubzero.org/groups/hubzero_hipaa/wiki/164308a1iiDInformationSystemActivityReview

title: Workforce Security
content:
Goal:

Implement policies and procedures to ensure that all members of its workforce have appropriate access to electronic protected health information, as provided under paragraph (a)(4) of this section, and to prevent those workforce members who do not have access under paragraph (a)(4) of this section from obtaining access to electronic protected health information.

Background

HUBzero staff that have administrative rights (“privileged access”) to the systems containing EPHI are covered by the following policies. That is because they could modify the system or application code that is used to store, process, transform, and/or modify EPHI and through that action expose the EPHI to unauthorized individuals. The exposure could be accidental (through a configuration change) or intentional (through modification of source code).
For example, being root or a member of www-data means that they can potentially capture the unencrypted EPHI as the forms are being submitted. Even after EPHI has been encrypted, the encryption key is available to people with this type of privileged access, so in effect they have full access. Superusers in the web interface at "/administrator". Paragraph (a) (4) Information Access Management policies and procedures define privileged access. “Workforce member” below refers to HUBzero staff only.


Authorization And/Or Supervision

1. HUBzero shall ensure that HUBzero workforce members who have the ability to access EPHI or work in areas where EPHI might be accessed, shall be properly authorized and/or supervised.


2. HUBzero will define and maintain processes for granting authorization and access to EPHI, including:

a. Procedure for permitting access to EPHI
b. Procedure for logging and tracking authorization of access to EPHI.
c. Procedure for reviewing and revising, on a periodic basis, authorization of access to EPHI (the periodic basis is to be defined in the documentation of that process).
The above are documented at 164.308 a 4 Information Access Management, Access Authorization.

3. Workforce members shall not be allowed access to EPHI or to areas where EPHI might be accessed until proper authorization is granted.

4. Only authorized workforce members who have need for privileged access in order to fulfill their respective job responsibilities shall be authorized to access EPHI or areas where EPHI might be accessed. HUBzero shall review access levels on a periodic basis and make revisions as necessary. HUBzero shall establish a procedure for reviewing and revising, on a periodic basis, authorization of access to EPHI or to areas where EPHI might be accessed.

The above-mentioned procedure is documented at 164.308 a 4 Information Access Management, Access Establishment and Modification.


Workforce Clearance Procedure


1. HUBzero shall take reasonable and appropriate steps to ensure that workforce members have the appropriate authorization to access EPHI.

See 164.308 a 4 Information Access Management, Access Authorization.

2. HUBzero managers, system administrators and the HIPAA liaison will work together to identify which HUBzero employees are allowed to grant privileged access to other workforce members or supervise them.


3. HUBzero will rely on SDSC Human Resources to review prospective workforce members’ backgrounds during the hiring process.


Policy for Termination Procedures

Detailed termination procedures are maintained at https://hubzero.org/groups/production/wiki/TerminationProcs

For the purposes of termination procedures, hubs have at least 2 kinds of users: SDSC employees and others.

San Diego Supercomputing Center (SDSC) Employees

Access privileges will be removed or disabled as soon as possible upon notification from an employee’s supervisor that the access is no longer needed. If the employee has ceased work and a public notice of termination is published before an employee’s supervisor or a hub owner specifies which access should be preserved, it must be assumed that no access is needed anymore.


Other employees

Access credentials of hub users that aren’t Purdue employees will be removed or disabled as soon as possible upon notification from a credible and authoritative source (e.g., the owner of a hub) that the access is no longer needed or that it should be withdrawn.

It should be noted that the objective of these termination procedures is not to remove all access, but to *reduce* access privileges to those enjoyed by regular hub users, unless complete removal is desired for disciplinary reasons (e.g., as a consequence of policy violations). Thus, accounts themselves should normally not be disabled or closed, although closing accounts used solely in the course of employment (e.g., test accounts) is appropriate. It is problematic to determine exactly which access a terminated employee should have as a regular hub user; when in doubt, group memberships and other privileges must be removed. Hub owners or group managers can later grant access back. The act of removing and granting access later based on the new, regular hub user status shows that due diligence was done and provides assurance that the access privileges are correct.

Responsibility for Applying the Termination Procedures

Hubzero staff are responsible for applying the policy for prior employees. Otherwise, hub owners and their staff are responsible for applying the policy for their own staff, students and anyone to whom they have granted privileges.

title: Information Access Management
content:
Goal

Implement policies and procedures for authorizing access to electronic protected health information that are consistent with the applicable requirements of subpart E of this part.

Definition

Privileged access to a HUBzero science gateway deployment is defined as having physical access to the underlying hardware, or administrative access to the virtualization layer, or any access to the "/administrator" pages of the web service, or any privilege on the operating system and the services it runs that exceeds that given automatically to people registering for an account on the science gateway using the interface provided to do so.  Examples of this are “superuser” access to the "/administrator" pages of the web service, root access to some layer of the infrastructure, being a member of an “access-” group (see role-based access controls for an explanation of the “access-” groups), or any combination of privileges allowing one to act as an account running an important service, or root. In effect, this privileged access either outright grants access to EPHI information, or potentially makes it easier to abuse flaws.

Access Authorization

a. Procedure for permitting access to EPHI.

The person granting privileged access must verify that the workforce member needs this access.

The person granting privileged access to a HIPAA-covered system must verify that the workforce member has taken appropriate HIPAA training.  This training shall satisfy the requirements of any parent organization under which HUBzero operates.

All hub user (CMS) account information is stored in LDAP and MySQL. Local user accounts can be used for administrators of the operating system that do not have hub accounts, or for development systems that do not handle HIPAA data. Otherwise, local accounts for people on HUBzero infrastructure systems must be kept to a minimum and their use must be justified, especially if this access may grant access to EPHI information.

The person granting privileged access must verify that any user’s mobile devices that will be used with HIPAA-covered hubs comply with the encryption policy (see “164.312 Technical Safeguards a Access Control”).

System accounts, that is, accounts used for running a system service or some other function such as running automated scripts, must not be associated with a particular person, and must not be used for login purposes by people.

b. Procedure for logging and tracking authorization of access to EPHI.

Tracking authorization of access to EPHI is done by gathering the list of users with established privileged access, as defined above. In other words, HUBzero uses the establishment of privileged access as a record of authorization.

c. Procedure for reviewing and revising, on a periodic basis, authorization of access to EPHI.

Every year, an audit will verify if workforce members that were authorized, have done or refreshed the required HIPAA training. Twice a year an audit will verify that they still need this access. Local accounts on HUBzero infrastructure which may grant access to EPHI information will also be reviewed.


Access Establishment and Modification


1. Process for establishing, documenting, reviewing, and modifying access to EPHI

a. Procedure for establishing and documenting access to EPHI.

This is done by granting privileged access as defined above, by the appropriate mechanism. Accesses to EPHI are not documented by HUBzero, and are the responsibility of the covered application or service hosted by SDSC HUBzero.

b. Procedure for documenting establishment of access to EPHI.

The establishment of access to EPHI, by itself, is not documented separately by HUBzero.

c. Procedure for reviewing on a regular basis workforce members’ access privileges to EPHI.

Every year, a list of which workforce members that have privileged access to systems with EPHI information will be made, both through local or central accounts. Authorization will then be verified, and access privileges modified accordingly.

d. Procedure for modifying the access privileges of workforce members to EPHI, as appropriate, based on the periodic reviews.

This is done by using the mechanism by which privileged access was granted, as described above.

2. Authorization and training of workforce members to access EPHI


a. Definition and classification of permitted access methods

Workforce members must use encrypted communication protocols (e.g., SSH) to access the systems and services for which they have privileged access. Clear text protocols (e.g., MySQL, telnet) are expressly forbidden. Workforce members will be shown how to use SSH for tunneling clear text protocols, therefore encrypting the communication.

b. Definition and classification of length of time access will be permitted.

Access will be permitted until a workforce member changes positions or an audit determines that their privileged access is not needed anymore.

c. Procedure for appropriate logging and tracking of activities by an authorized workforce member on EPHI.

Activities of workforce members with privileged access are tracked the same on all HUBzero infrastructure regardless of whether EPHI is involved. HUBzero tracks logins via SSH and the web server.

 

Previous versions of this policy are available in the old wiki at https://help.hubzero.org/groups/hubzero_hipaa/wiki/164308a4InformationAccessManagement

title: Security Awareness and Training
content:
1. Security Reminders

HUBzero will post security reminders in its Slack workspace, in the "general" channel, reminding the workforce on the importance of protecting PHI.  The HUBzero ISO will select security reminders from blog posts relevant to current activity at HUBzero, from hipaasecuritysuite.com (see https://hipaasecuritysuite.com/hipaa-compliant-security-reminders), or from other appropriate souces.

System administrators will subscribe to at least one security mailing list relevant to the operating systems and software in use.

2. Protection From Malicious Software

2.1 Practices and procedures for malware prevention and detection

The following practices and procedures are to be taught to system administrators, as described in section 2.3. HUBzero infrastructure will be setup to automatically check for malware where appropriate by using:

  • Intrusion detection software
  • Anti-virus software (e.g., ClamAV)

2.1.1 Intrusion detection software

HUBzero shall rely on intrusion detection software selected and installed in the Sherlock environment.  In other environments, "Rootkit Hunter" will be deployed.  It (http://www.rootkit.nl/) aims to detect rootkits typically installed after a compromise. Scans shall be run at least weekly and whenever a compromise is suspected.

2.1.2 Anti-virus software

In the Sherlock environment, the anti-virus software is installed and managed by the Sherlock team as described in the Sherlock System Security Plan.  Any functionality described below that isn't covered by the Sherlock anti-virus solution, will be covered as described below.  In other environments:

a. Updates of anti-virus signatures

The anti-virus ClamAV signatures must be updated at least daily.  Normally this is done automatically by clamav-freshclam.

b. Downloadable resources

A weekly cron script must trigger a ClamAV scan of a hub's downloadable resources, and report any findings via email to system administrators.  System administrators must determine if the results are valid and remove infected files.

c. Incoming mail

Mail server software (e.g., exim, postfix) must be configured to scan incoming emails with an anti-virus such as ClamAV, and reject emails and attachments containing detected malware.

d. HTTP Uploads

The HUBzero science gateway web application must use the ClamAV daemon to automatically scan HTTP(S) uploads on the fly, and reject uploads containing detected malware.

e. Home directories of users

The home directories of users must be scanned monthly for malware with ClamAV.  It isn't practical to use a shorter scanning interval because on some hubs, scanning home directories takes more than a week.  Detected malware will either be deleted by a system administrator, or the user will be notified of the issue.  If by the next scan, the user hasn't taken action, a system administrator will delete the infected files.

 

2.2 What to do about malicious software

In the Sherlock HIPAA environment, malicious software will be handled by the Sherlock team as described in Sherlock policies.  Outside of it:

a. How to report malicious software

All events that may constitute IT Incidents should be reported to abuse@help.hubzero.org , and escalated to parent organizations as needed. More details on what constitutes an IT Incident and what to report are described in the HUBzero Incident Response Plan.

b. How to recover from malicious software

Once an infection has been determined to have occurred, the infected system should be taken offline (shutdown) as soon as possible. The ongoing risks to other infrastructure and users are a greater concern to HUBzero than the preservation of evidence achieved by examining the live system.

Malicious software can be extremely resistant to removal. Most often, wiping the hard drive, re-partitioning and complete OS installation from a trusted source is required, or is more effective than trying to fight the malware. The time necessary to decide whether this is required is often better spent in performing the procedure. However, HUBzero system administrators should attempt to determine the method by which the malicious software was installed. This is better done by looking at backups. Once a counter-measure has been determined, it should be applied to existing systems as well as to the rebuilt one as soon as possible.

2.3 Training

Developers are encouraged to attend security tracks at conferences, pursue independent reading and watch webcasts. In addition, the "UC Learning Center" offers a large number of security-related classes that all HUBzero staff should pursue.  A record of security training will be kept at https://help.hubzero.org/groups/policies/wiki/sec_training

The previously described practices and procedures will be taught to HUBzero system administrators. This will be done by assigned reading of this wiki and discussion.

3. Login Monitoring

Given that HUBzero has been designed as a 24/7 research environment; that accesses can presumably and justifiably occur at any time 24/7, and have been observed to occur at any time; that users include neophytes that often forget passwords and require many attempts for a valid login; that HUBzero workforce members have little knowledge of the habits of the clientele of a particular hub; login discrepancies are extremely difficult to identify and any such identification is error-prone. Therefore, HUBzero will make available to hub owners web login data and SSH login data on the systems belonging to that hub. Hub owners are responsible for monitoring logins to applications manipulating EPHI, and identifying discrepancies.

HUBzero’s contribution to login monitoring will be limited to providing automated protection against password guessing attacks.  This currently takes the form of temporary account lockout supplemented by the banning of IP addresses responsible for the lockout of several accounts.  Procedures to configure the lockout parameters and temporary bans will be documented.

4. Password Management

This is addressed by UCSD policy via the yearly "UC Cyber Security Awareness" training. Hubs deploying custom applications and Hub partners with other software are responsible for reminding users about password protection when accessing EPHI information.

title: Audit Control
content:
Goals

Implement hardware, software, and/or procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in information systems that contain or use electronic protected health information.

Review

This policy and related procedures shall be reviewed at least every 3 years.

Mixed Responsibility

For HIPAA-covered systems, the Sherlock environment provides logging and auditing capabilities and policies that supplement, and in some cases, replace, the normal SDSC HUBzero policies.  In those cases, SDSC HUBzero is responsible for auditing related to the operation of HUBzero web application science gateway itself;  SDSC Sherlock is responsible for all other auditing, e.g., operating system-level events, anti-virus software activity, etc...

Auditable Events (AU-2)

HUBzero deployments must be capable of auditing the following events, defined by control AU-2, and must have procedures to do so:

  • Server alerts and error messages
  • User log-on and log-off (successful or unsuccessful;
  • System administration activities;
  • Modification of privileges and access
  • Start up and shut down
  • Modifications to the application
  • Application alerts and error messages
  • Configuration changes
  • Account creation, modification, or deletion

The system has the capability to log events as provided by all Linux OS distributions and included software packages.  In addition, the HUBzero software can log authentication events, as well as access requests and the HTTP result code for the requests.  General usage inside the HUBzero software is logged in the database table "jos_activity_logs".  This is supplemented with additional logging implemented by "components".  Each software component is responsible for defining more specific auditable events and logging their use in additional database tables.

Which events are relevant is a function of HUBzero’s primary goals, which are to restore integrity and availability and protect confidentiality. Providing forensic evidence for law enforcement's use isn’t a concern although it may happen incidentally. As a defense against compromise, all authentication attempts (successes and failures) across all mechanisms supported by the Apache web service should be logged, including use of cookies, WebDAV, or SVN over HTTP. Repeated failures should result in bans to protect against brute force attacks, except where implemented separately for federated identity providers.  Bans are auditable events, to address availability complaints and ensure the proper function of the mechanism.

For availability purposes, mail (SMTP) events should be logged. The IP addresses of servers attempting to deliver spam should also be logged to block repeated attempts to abuse the mail system.

Similarly, SSH activity should be logged and processed to automatically block repeated attacks, as well as flag that activity. 

Content of Audit Records (AU-3)

HUBzero deployments must generate audit records containing information that establishes what type of event occurred, when the event occurred, where the event occurred, the source of the event, the outcome of the event, and the identity of any individuals or subjects associated with the event (see control AU-3).  All authentication attempts (successes and failures) across all mechanisms supported by the Apache web service are logged, including use of cookies, WebDAV, SVN over HTTP. Repeated failures result in bans to protect against brute force attacks, except for Google and Shibboleth because these authentication mechanisms have their own protection mechanisms. Bans are logged with the time and IP address, and in the case of an account suspension, which user account was implicated.

HUBzero software logs usernames, IP addresses, URLs accessed, time, protocol used (e.g., version of TLS), and the nature of the events (e.g., password changes, failed access, Google authentication, Shibboleth records, and bans).  The default logging format of other services is used.

HUBzero also logs mail (SMTP) events. The IP addresses of servers attempting to deliver spam are also logged to block repeated attempts to abuse the mail system. HUBzero also logs all requests made to the web server, which are processed with regular expressions to detect unusual activity and automatically block some forms of attacks (e.g., SQL injection). Similarly, SSH activity is logged and processed with regular expressions to automatically block repeated attacks, as well as flag that activity in automated emails sent to administrators.

Audit Storage Capacity (AU-4)

HUBzero relies on the virtual environments where it is deployed to provide disk space as needed (e.g., SDSC Sherlock, SDSC RDS and AWS).

historical, for reference only: 

HUBzero uses LVM to flexibly manage storage space, in combination with monitoring of storage status every 5 minutes and alarms with the Xymon system. The Xymon system monitors the disk space available for logs, and sends alerts when reaching 90 (yellow) and 95 (red) percent capacity. Storage organization follows CIS benchmark suggestions to separate audit storage from data storage, making the whole more robust against failures, abuses, and unexpected usage levels. A pool of spare storage that can be assigned as needed is available. Audit storage has a capacity that exceeds previously encountered peak levels by at least 10%.

Response to Audit Processing Failures (AU-5)

When running out of storage space, the logging mechanisms used by HUBzero deployments, including needed services as well as the HUBzero software, must discard the oldest event logs so new activity can still be logged (see control AU-5).

Time Stamps (AU-8)

HUBzero records timestamp information at a granularity of 1 second. Time is synchronized using a stratum 1 server. Synchronization status is monitored by the Xymon system.

Retention (AU-11)

As a baseline, standard Linux OS and service logs (e.g., Apache) must be collected for 30 days and retained for up to 1 year through the use of monthly backup images.  Database tables used for logging must also collect data for 30 days, relying on monthly backup images to provide log access for up to a year.  If a hub is retired (no longer in production service), only one recent backup will be kept for up to a year.

AU-12 Audit Generation

HUBzero deployments must:

a. Provide audit record generation capability for the auditable events defined in AU-2 for components and services managed by HUBzero;

b. Allow System Administrators and CMS administrators, as applicable, to select which auditable events are to be audited by specific components of the information system; and

c. Generate audit records for the events defined in AU-2 d. with the content defined in AU-3.

Hardware Mechanisms

A central logging stand-alone host is used to receive logs and process them.  In addition to local copies are kept on the servers, and more copies kept on backup servers.  All copies contribute to log retention.

Software and Procedural Mechanisms (excluding Sherlock environment):

On UNIX servers, system activity is logged in various files in the directory /var/log, which are examined by the fail2ban mechanism. Excessive failures result in a ban of the IP address concerned, with a different sensitivity depending on whether the address belongs to the HUBzero network or if it is external. This applies to both web site logins (including WebDAV) and SSH logins (including sftp). Suspicious network activity also results in a ban of the IP addresses involved.

Historical, for reference only (not in place at SDSC): 

Information gathered from system logs shall be automatically and periodically filtered by blacklisting known routine events representing normal activity, and sending for review all other events to system administrators.  In addition, a monitoring system shall be used to log resource usage and relevant indicators of system activity.

All events received by a system's logging mechanism (whether rsyslog, system-journald or other) shall be filtered as described above.  On HIPAA-covered hubs, a system administrator shall also review Apache access and error logs using a similar filter.

The syslog records are sent to a centralized logging system. There, activity deemed normal is automatically filtered out using logcheck software, and everything else is emailed to system administrators on an hourly basis. Administrators on duty are expected to read these emails, looking for signs of trouble.

Reviews shall be done every hour if possible, and at least once every regular business day. It is sufficient that a single system administrator does this, but it is OK to have more. System administrators are responsible for coordinating this.

All system administrators must receive these emails, which contains log events triaged and filtered through the logcheck software. Only email accounts hosted on Purdue systems or a provider nationally recognized for secure email (e.g., Gmail) shall be used for subscribing to the list.

The Apache logs are filtered locally through logcheck software, and reports of unexpected activity are emailed hourly to administrators. 

CMS administrators are responsible for monitoring the PHP error log files. The PHP error logs are automatically monitored by size, and sudden increases result in alerts sent to CMS administrators.  CMS administrators are responsible for reacting to these emails and handling the related issues.

A designated HUBzero system administrator must be reachable via telephone and answer calls from Purdue IOC outside business hours.  After such a call, system administrators must:
        make a best effort attempt at resolving the situation
        Report findings that may affect customer experiences, or that may be of interest, to the entire HUBzero team using a Slack channel.
        Given Slack messages, gateway managers will contact Hub owners and appropriate external staff as required.
