title: (SC) Systems and Communications Protection
content:
This is not a policy document. 

This document describes implementation details for controls, i.e., control requirements in comparison to implementation status in relation to responsibilities of HUBzero and the providers of the environments we are using (e.g., Sherlock).

SC-1 System and Communications Protection Policy and Procedures

Current Implementation Details:

This policy is documented in the SDSC Sherlock System Security Plan.  HUBzero complies with this control with its Incident Response Plan,  Disaster Recovery Plan, and other systematically developed policies and procedures to cover HIPAA requirements. Communications protection is specifically covered under the HUBzero policy “164.312 Technical Safeguards, e Transmission Security” available at https://help.hubzero.org/documentation/itppr/policies/mapping-to-national-standards-and-regulations/hipaa-view/164312-technical-safeguards/164312-e-transmission-security .

SC-5 Denial of Service Protection

Control Description:

The information system protects against or limits the effects of the following types of denial of service attacks:

  • Internet Control Message Protocol (ICMP) floods:
    • Smurf attack
    • Ping of death
    • Ping flood
  • Teardrop attack
  • Peer-to-peer attacks
  • Permanent DoS attack (i.e., phlashing)
  • Application level floods:
    • Internet Relay Chat (IRC) floods
    • Banana attack
    • Buffer overflow
  • Nuke
  • Distributed DoS attack
  • Reflected attack
  • Unintentional attack
  • DoS Level II

Note: NIH and the ICs refers to the NIST SP 800-61, Computer Security Incident Handling Guide and timely industry information on denial of service attacks to define additional and update existing security safeguards, as required.

Current Implementation Details:

The Sherlock SSP states that: "Customer compute systems are located on separate physical or logical systems from Sherlock management systems. VLAN and firewall segmentation shall be used to partition the network traffic and access of the different customer computing systems from Sherlock management systems. For Cloud systems virtualization will be performed using cloud virtualization tools (e.g., AWS Virtual Private Network (VPC))."  Preventative measures described in the HUBzero Incident Response Plan also harden the VMs received from Sherlock, setting the appropriate Linux kernel networking options, and implementing appropriate host firewall rules.

 

SC-13 Cryptographic Protection

The information system implements cryptographic mechanisms as defined in the HHS Standard for Encryption of Computing Devices and Information in accordance with applicable federal laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, and standards.

Current Implementation Details:

The Sherlock SSP states that the "environment shall only use FIPS-validated cryptography products."  The HUBzero policy "164.312 e Transmission Security" implements best practices related to this control.

SC-15 Collaborative Computing Devices

The information system:
a. Prohibits remote activation of collaborative computing devices with no exceptions; and
b. Provides an explicit indication of use to users physically present at the devices.

Current Implementation Details:

The Sherlock SSP states that "use of remote control software is prohibited within the Sherlock environment. Use of collaborative computing devices (network white boards, cameras, microphones, etc.) is also prohibited within the Sherlock network."  The HUBzero web application has no knowledge of or control over the client selected by users.

title: (SI) System and Information Integrity
content:
This is not a policy document. 

This document provides the implementation status for controls, in relation to responsibilities of HUBzero and the providers of the environments we are using (e.g., Sherlock).

For HIPAA-covered hubs, please refer to the SDSC Sherlock System Security Plan as well.  The HUBzero controls below apply to all hubs unless contradicted by the Sherlock SSP or unapplicable or irrelevant due to the controls implemented in the Sherlock environment.

 

SI-1 System and Information Integrity Policy and Procedures

The HUBzero policy "164.312 c Integrity" mandates the implementation of control SI-1.  See the HUBzero Incident Response Plan under "3.2.3 Detective Measures": monitoring, anti-virus, scans, hashes

SI-2 Flaw Remediation

Control description:

The organization:
a. Identifies, reports, and corrects information system flaws;
b. Tests software and firmware updates related to flaw remediation for effectiveness and potential side effects before installation;
c. Installs security-relevant software and firmware updates promptly, in accordance with the note below, of the release of the updates; and
d. Incorporates flaw remediation into the organizational configuration management process.

Note: The timelines to remediate vulnerabilities is designated by the NIH Information Security Program. The following remediation timelines must be met, or the affected device may be removed from the network:
• Critical within 30 days;
• High within 60 days;
• Medium within 1 year; and
• Low within 1 year.

Implementation details

The HUBzero policy "164.312 c Integrity" mandates the implementation of control SI-2.  This is addressed in the Incident Response Plan, "3.3 Preventative Measures":Software Updates, as well as the policy on "Code Deployment" at https://help.hubzero.org/documentation/itppr/code-deployment.  The procedure for web application vulnerability scanning is documented at https://help.hubzero.org/documentation/itppr/procedures/technical/web-application-vulnerability-scanning along with the timelines required by this control.

Historical, for reference only: 

In the Purdue environment with Ogre configuration control, all patches are automatically applied the day of the release to non-production systems. Updates are checked daily, and the patches are applied next business day manually.

SI-3 Malicious Code Protection

Control description:

The organization:
a. Employs malicious code protection mechanisms at information system entry and exit points to detect and eradicate malicious code;
b. Updates malicious code protection mechanisms whenever new releases are available in accordance with organizational configuration management policy and procedures;
c. Configures malicious code protection mechanisms to:
1. Perform periodic scans of the information system at least monthly and real-time scans of files from external sources at endpoint and network entry/exit points as the files are downloaded, opened, or executed in accordance with organizational security policy; and
2. Executes one or more of the following in response to malicious code detection:
• Blocks malicious code
• Quarantines malicious code
• Sends an alert to the System Administrator; and
d. Addresses the receipt of false positives during malicious code detection and eradication and the resulting potential impact on the availability of the information system.

Note: Malicious code protection can include, for example, anti-virus agents and signature definitions, as well as reputation-based technologies.

Implementation details

The Sherlock environment is protected by a deployment of Sentinel One as described in the Sherlock System Security Plan (SSP).  In addition, the HUBzero science gateway web application uses ClamAV as described in policy "a 5 Security Awareness and Training", in section "2. Protection From Malicious Software".  The combination meets the requirements of this control.

SI-4 System and Information Integrity

Control description:

The organization:
a. Monitors the information system to detect:
1. Attacks and indicators of potential attacks in accordance with NIH and IC monitoring objectives as described AU-2 and AU-5(2) and
2. Unauthorized local, network, and remote connections (For Moderate and High systems: twice weekly);
b. Identifies unauthorized use of the information system through NIH and/or IC techniques and methods as described in AU-6 and AU-7(1);
c. Deploys monitoring devices: (i) strategically within the information system to collect organization-determined essential information; and (ii) at ad hoc locations within the system to track specific types of transactions of interest to the organization;
d. Protects information obtained from intrusion-monitoring tools from unauthorized access, modification, and deletion;
e. Heightens the level of information system monitoring activity whenever there is an indication of increased risk to organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, or the Nation based on law enforcement information, intelligence information, or other credible sources of information;
f. Obtains legal opinion with regard to information system monitoring activities in accordance with applicable federal laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, or regulations; and
g. Provides information system monitoring information to NIH Threat Mitigation and Incident Response (TMIR) and System Owners and IC ISSO, System Owners, and security personnel at either an as needed basis and/or, at a minimum, twice weekly for Moderate and High systems.

Implementation details

The HUBzero policy "164.312 c Integrity" mandates the implementation of control SI-4.

SI-5 Security Alerts and Advisories

Control description:

The organization:
a. Receives information system security alerts, advisories, and directives from the United States Computer Emergency Readiness Team (US-CERT) on an ongoing basis;
b. Generates internal security alerts, advisories, and directives as deemed necessary;
c. Disseminates security alerts, advisories, and directives to NIH CIO, CISO, TMIR and IC CIO, ISSO, System Owner, and security personnel; and
d. Implements security directives in accordance with established time frames or notifies the issuing organization of the degree of noncompliance.

Implementation details

The HUBzero policy "164.312 c Integrity" mandates the implementation of control SI-5.  See Incident Response Plan, "3.3 Preventative Measures": Advisories. 

SI-12 Information Handling and Retention

Control description:

The organization handles and retains information within the information system and information output from the system in accordance with applicable federal laws, Executive Orders, directives, policies, regulations, standards, and operational requirements.

Implementation details

The HUBzero policy "164.312 c Integrity" mandates the implementation of control SI-12.

title: Metadata and Privacy
content:
The Metadata Information Leakage Problem

Vulnerability scanners report the presence of metadata in images served by web servers.  This includes several types of metadata, such as Exif, which can reveal dates, GPS coordinates, and more, which are details that may not have been indended to be published, and may have consequences similar to "doxing".

Hubs have a more complicated situation than a basic web site because they contain and republish data;  the metadata may matter and even be part of the scientific value of the data and publications that a hub curates. Data creators and owners are best positioned to identify which metadata has value, and which present privacy risks. Hubs are typically curators without the information and manpower necessary to make decisions about the metadata. Therefore, the metadata must be filtered before being uploaded. To bring awareness of this issue, hubs shall include by default the following sentences in their published privacy policy:

"Users are responsible for any privacy issues consequent to uploading files containing metadata (e.g., images with GPS coordinates). Users are responsible for stripping metadata, as appropriate, before uploading files."

title: Network Services Policy
content:
Plain text protocols are easy targets of attacks and their use is discouraged and restricted. 

  • NFSv3 must be limited to HUBzero networks within the same datacenter, as enforced by our network firewalls;  servers must restrict access by the IP address of specific clients and use read-only exports and root_squash whenever possible (a bug in the RHEL kernel in RHEL 6 requires the no_root_squash option for /home).
  • Plain text MySQL connections may be allowed for read-only access to databases that have no sensitive information, and clients must reside within hubzero networks, unless the database server is hosted by someone else (in which case it's their problem and their policy applies).  Network firewalls must enforce this.  An example where this is allowed is the geolocation database on hubzero.org (the only one allowed at the time of writing this policy). 
  • Other MySQL connections must be secured via SSH local port forwarding where the destination server is also the SSH server, or by forcing SSL encryption in the MySQL configuration (see procedure for securing MySQL).
  • iSCSI services must specify different users and passwords for incoming and outgoing connections (IncomingUser and OutgoingUser settings), and those must also be different for each target.  iSCSI connections must be limited to the specific IP address of the clients.  They must also be limited to within a datacenter, unless SSH port forwarding where the destination server is also the SSH server is used to secure the connection.  Network firewalls must enforce this as well.
  • Telnet as a service is forbidden.  Both host and network firewalls must enforce this. 
  • Host and network firewalls must block access to services by default unless a valid use case exists.

For encrypted communications, ciphers and MAC algorithms must be selected to exclude broken or weak algorithms.  Network vulnerability scans can identify some of them.  Refer also to NIST standards and available test suites and benchmarks to identify acceptable protocols.  For example, Qualys SSL Labs offers an SSL server test identifying weak algorithms.  Other organizations also publish guidelines that can be consulted for insight, such as mozilla.org (see https://wiki.mozilla.org/Security/Guidelines/OpenSSH).

Protocols that don't provide sufficient encryption and protection against attacks must not be used over the internet unless tunneled, but might be used locally.  Example: SMBv3.

title: Secure Programming
content:
Software security flaws can be introduced at  any stage of the software development lifecycle, including:   

  • Not identifying security requirements up front
  • Creating conceptual designs that have logic errors
  • Using poor coding practices that introduce technical vulnerabilities
  • Deploying the software improperly  
  • Introducing flaws during maintenance or updating

Security by Design

Security needs to be a priority as you develop code, not an afterthought. Organizations may have competing priorities where software engineering and coding are concerned. Optimizing for security can conflict with optimizing for development speed. However, a “security by design” approach that puts security first tends to pay off in the long run, reducing the future cost of technical debt and risk mitigation. An analysis of your source code should be conducted throughout your SDLC, and security automation  implemented.  Both are in place.

Password Management

  • Store passwords and credentials only is specified locations by the Hubzero Security Officer.
  • Protect passwords and credentials per the policy and procedures for the credentials storage system.
  • Never save a password, key, or other credential in a code repository.

Access Control

Take a “default deny” approach to sensitive data. Limit privileges and restrict access to secure data to only users who need it. Deny access to any user that cannot demonstrate authorization. Ensure that requests for sensitive information are checked to verify that the user is authorized to access it. 

Error Handling and Logging

Software errors are often indicative of bugs, many of which cause vulnerabilities. Error handling and logging are two of the most useful techniques for minimizing their impact. Error handling attempts to catch errors in the code before they result in a catastrophic failure. Logging documents errors so that developers can diagnose and mitigate their cause. 

Documentation and logging of all failures, exceptions, and errors should be implemented on a trusted system to comply with secure coding standards.

For example, could there be an error that would return an empty page or make Apache send HTTP code 200?

Threat Modeling

Document, locate, address, and validate are the four steps to threat modeling. To securely code, you need to examine your software for areas susceptible to increased threats of attack. Threat modeling is a multi-stage process that should be integrated into the software lifecycle from development, testing, and production. 

Cryptographic Practices

Using quality modern cryptographic algorithms with keys stored in secure key vaults is a practice that increases the security of your code in the event of a breach.

Input Validation and Output Encoding

These secure coding standards are self-explanatory in that you need to identify all data inputs and sources and validate those classified as untrusted. You should utilize a standard routine for output encoding and input validation. Don't assume that because you set a value, e.g., in a "hidden input", it is still safe to use after going through the client browser! In other words, can you absolutely guarantee that a variable is safe to use?  If not, systematically verify it with input validation.

Adopt a secure coding standard.

Develop and apply a secure coding standard for your target development language and platform.

Use effective quality assurance techniques.

Good quality assurance techniques can be effective in identifying and eliminating vulnerabilities. Fuzz testing, penetration testing, and source code audits should all be incorporated as part of an effective quality assurance program. Independent security reviews can lead to more secure systems.


Check the OWASP top ten issues

Verify that your web application code won't be vulnerable to any of the issues described at https://owasp.org/www-project-top-ten/

Reference Guide

A reference guide https://owasp.org/www-pdf-archive/OWASP_Code_Review_Guide_v2.pdf

title: Termination Policy
content:
People who are no longer employees or who change positions, but retain access privileges, create risks for organizations.   Therefore, typical termination procedures revoke all access privileges before an employee has the opportunity to cause problems.  However, HUBzero offers public services, so our termination procedures have for goal to remove access beyond what a normal user would get, instead of removing all access.  An exception is when an employee is discharged for Serious Misconduct (see definition in the Purdue Separation Pay policy at http://www.purdue.edu/policies/human-resources/vif1.html) or when policy violations are implicated, in which case additional or complete removal of access is appropriate.  Hub test accounts are to be deleted during termination procedures because regular users should have only one account per the normal Terms of Use, unless a Hub has modified such terms of use to allow multiple accounts per individual.

For the purposes of this policy, hubs have at least 2 kinds of users: HUBzero employees and others.

1. HUBzero Employees

Purdue sends notices of employee termination monthly, named "Terminations, Transfers, Hires, Rehires" from "staffchgs@lists.purdue.edu" in .xlsx format.   Processing this is exceedingly slow and painful, with the monthly interval carrying considerable security risks.  HUBzero employees and supervisors must adhere to this Termination Policy, as well as devise procedures in such a way that HUBzero may justifiably be excused from using and relying on these notices. 

  • Supervisors MUST notify both system and CMS administrators PROMPTLY, as soon as an employee is terminated or has started work elsewhere or in a different position, if not already done. 
  • If known ahead of time, supervisors SHOULD notify system and CMS administrators 2-5 business days in advance when an employee will be terminated or will be hired in a different position.  This will allow preparing for the change, and clarifying any issues.
  • If hired in a different position at Purdue, the previous and new supervisors MUST specify the new roles of the employee with respect to HUBzero, from which access privileges will be derived.
  • If terminated, all access privileges beyond those offered to the public will be removed unless the supervisor specifies an exception.  Exceptions must include an expiration date and a justification.
  • If system or CMS administrators learn of an employee termination through a public announcement or some other credible source before a supervisor contacts them, they must attempt to confirm with the supervisor.  If unable to contact the supervisor or get a response within 4 hours, they MUST start termination procedures as soon as is practical.
  • System and CMS administrators MUST promptly complete termination procedures, as soon as is practical, and plan to start them so they are completed the end of the last working day of the employee.
  • If an employee leaving HUBzero employment contributes to the termination procedures (e.g., by removing oneself's from groups), the final state of access privileges MUST be verified by someone else after completion of the termination procedures.

2. Others

Hub owners and managers are responsible for elevated privileges who have been granted to other users, and for seeing them removed at termination time. Hub owners and managers MUST:

  • Promptly remove users from groups managed in the HUBzero software ("CMS") when the membership is no longer appropriate, and demote the access level of such users in the CMS (e.g., superuser).
  • Notify HUBzero as soon as users do not need elevated privileges in the OS, e.g., any access granted through the "access request" administrative procedure.  This includes the removal of privileges as a consequence of policy violations.

title: Web Server Filesystem Security Model
content:
DRAFT

The current version of the filesystem security model is at https://help.hubzero.org/resources/1370/supportingdocs .  It will likely stay there for practical reasons.

 

-----------------------------------------------------------

Web server security has many different aspects.  This document focuses on how file access permissions are managed, depending on user roles.

Version: 1.16, September 2017

Author: Pascal Meunier

Status: Draft, copy from the Policy group resources is in progress

1. Motivation and Scope

Change control and change management improve the availability (uptime) of production systems. The more there are people who can make uncoordinated changes, the greater the potential for disruption, downtime, and undesirable events. This document aims to define who can make changes to what based on their responsibilities (roles), as a foundation to security and change control. To do so it will emphasize accountability and discipline. This document is not a complete change management strategy, but rather describes the application of well-known security principles to HUBzero systems:

  • The principle of least privilege requires that users have the access and capabilities required for the performance of their duties and only those. It prevents some accidents and abuse, as well as actions performed by people without the appropriate training. It also reduces risk, should a user account get compromised.

  • The principle of separation of duties requires the cooperation of two people or more to make critical changes. This aims to reduce risk from a single user account getting compromised, mistakes made by a single user, or from a subverted or disgruntled employee attempting sabotage or other violation of policies.

We have seen the alternative, as without this security model all privileges were conflated into membership into the www-data group. This membership was all-powerful, allowing modifications to the web site (/www), accessing multiple logs, allowing logins on web servers, reading database account credentials which in turn give access to authentication information for all users; and changing configuration files, even if an individual required only minor access. The group membership was controlled by the CMS, so a compromise at the CMS level could be exploited to gain elevated privileges over the filesystem.  There is also a tendency for CMS superadmins to add themselves and their friends to the www-data group, and for convenience to supplant security. As a result, people have the capability to modify all PHP code whereas all some need is the ability to read some logs, or modify the contents of a single directory (supergroup managers).  We observed modifications made directly to CMS files by HUB owners, their staff, and students which work for them, which caused headaches later. The problem is compounded by the takeover of LDAP management by the CMS, which makes the capability to change the PHP code very powerful -- all account information is vulnerable.

Another reason to adopt this model is that not all accounts that were given www-data memberships were owned by real people. For example, the "splunk" account on a hub was in www-data based solely on the need to read log files. This meant that a compromise of the "splunk" account could potentially grant full access to the CMS. This defeated the purpose of using separate accounts for different system services, a foundation of UNIX security and an application of the separation of duties principle.

In the following, we will enumerate the tasks commonly accomplished on hubs, and define a mechanism granting the capabilities needed to perform these tasks.  By grouping the capabilities into roles, and assigning roles to individuals, people can be granted uniform and systematic sets of capabilities that are justified by their responsibilities.  Roles standardize permissions for well understood and defined sets of activities. This makes the granted privileges more easily understandable, consistent and therefore auditable, providing assurance.

 

1.1 Implementation and Responsibility

  • Gateway Community Managers or Science Gateway Managers (previously Hub Liaisons) are responsible for educating hub owners and users about this policy, and as needed for filing tickets to grant and remove roles for people who aren't directly HUBzero employees.
  • Hubzero system administrators are responsible for following and enforcing the procedures described in this document.
  • People involved in deploying code or creating packages are responsible for setting appropriate permissions and ownership on directories and files.  To avoid race conditions, this should be done by setting appropriate umasks instead of first writing the file insecurely and later fixing the permissions, and by copying the files using a process with the correct ownership instead of first copying with elevated privileges and then fixing ownership.

 

1.2 Short Document History

The first versions of this document were of a white paper titled "HUBzero Web Server Security Model", with a suggested implementation plan. The model and policies described therein were first implemented at the beginning of January 2014, and the transition for all hubs managed by HUBzero was complete as of April 2014.

This document was edited and the title changed in September 2014 to “Web Server Security Model: Filesystem”, after a review and engagement with the Center for Trustworthy Scientific Cyberinfrastructure (CTSC).

A new role was added in August 2015, metrics curator (a.k.a. “data science engineer”), because the DBA role was insufficient and a person in charge of metrics had been given full root access in the absence of a proper set of permissions and group memberships.

Version 1.15 was renamed "Groups and Roles".

Version 1.16 (current) updated and copied the policy to the "documentation" area of help.hubzero.org.  Prior to that, versions were stored as a resource of the "policy" group at https://help.hubzero.org/resources/1370/supportingdocs .

 

2. Executive Summary

After consultation with interested parties and identifying the reasons why people require www-data membership, I identified useful roles. The roles grant capabilities through Operating System groups memberships. This allows reasoning about the capabilities people need for their responsibilities, while applying principles of least privilege and separation of duties. In addition, by granting group memberships at the host's operating system level (/etc/group) instead of CMS/LDAP, an appropriate review and expiration of privileges can take place. This addresses the problem of self-granting privileges using the CMS, or granting to friends or students that don't have the appropriate training, skills, or goals.

3. Mechanism

Users are assigned roles in the configuration management system (Ogre or Ansible).  These roles are translated into group memberships.  These groups have gids lower than those used by the HUBzero software.  The operating system ignores LDAP information for gids in that range.  Therefore, control of LDAP information by the HUBzero software can't be leveraged to elevate privileges inappropriately on the filesystem.  Groups either are used directly for directory and file ownership, or are used as checks in service configurations or to grant sudo capabilities.

4. Required Capabilities

title: Procedures
content: How we want things to be done.  Procedures are the implementation of policies or must conform to policies.  Procedures are more than just "how-to" but also include checks and safeguards to prevent or detect undesirable outcomes, handle correctly corner cases, and provide proof that they were done correctly at the right time.  Documented procedures not only save time but provide assurance.

title: Administrative
content:
These procedures aim to describe mainly administrative processes that need to take place, such as authorization.

  • Access Control

  • Support

title: Access to Purdue Resources Through  PWL_319_HUBzero_DNS Groups
content:
Access to Purdue firewall contexts and the BlueCat DNS system is managed through membership in the following groups.  Purdue has created 3 groups:

  • PWL_319_HUBzero_DNS_Approvers  (Unix groupname: h0dnsapp)
  • PWL_319_HUBzero_DNS_Requesters (h0dnsreq)
  • PWL_319_HUBzero_DNS_Read_Only  (h0dnsro)

to help manage HUBzero access to Purdue resources:

  • BlueCat DNS
    • communityhub.purdue.edu
    • purduenext.purdue.edu
    • DHCP service on the staff network (128.46.16.0/24)
    • Any other DNS "A" record pointing to our IP ranges
  • Network Firewall contexts
    • hubzero-dc-fw.tcom.purdue.edu (datacenters)
    • hubzero-vrf-fw.tcom.purdue.edu (staff)

Change requests need to be sent to accounts@purdue.edu.

Current memberships can be checked with ldapsearch on the central Purdue server (central.purdue.lcl, also named wppcendc02.itap.purdue.edu):

 

for gr in PWL_319_HUBzero_DNS_Approvers PWL_319_HUBzero_DNS_Requesters PWL_319_HUBzero_DNS_Read_Only; do
  echo $gr
  env LDAPTLS_REQCERT=demand ldapsearch -H ldaps://wppcendc02.itap.purdue.edu -LLL -b dc=central,dc=purdue,dc=lcl
  -xWD pmeunier@CENTRAL.PURDUE.LCL cn=$gr member
  echo
done

Note: this may fail due to LDAPTLS_REQCERT=demand if you don't have the needed root CA certificates installed.  See the SSL cert used by the LDAP server with:

 

openssl s_client -showcerts -connect wppcendc02.itap.purdue.edu:636 </dev/null

title: Access Request Procedure
content:
This procedure is to request elevated privileges or SSH access directly to a host without being constrained to SFTP or Virtual SSH.  It depends on the type of host you need access to.

Definitions

Host types

Multiple hosts may be provided in your hosting solution. Hosts are classified as one of the following:

  • Development
  • Testing
  • Staging
  • Quality Assurance (QA)
  • Pre-Production
  • User Acceptance Test Environment (UAT)
  • Production
  • HUBzero Infrastructure

In addition, hosts can be HIPAA-covered or not.  Only HUBzero staff will be given access to infrastructure hosts. 

Access Request

A written note submitted as a support ticket requesting an change in access for a specified user. See the Requirements section for the required information to be provided.

User

The person to which the access will be granted.

Requester

The person requesting access. May not be the same person that will be granted the access, but in many cases the Requester an User are same person.

Supervisor

The person ultimately responsible for the User’s action with the granted access. Must also provide written approval for the User to be granted access.

Development Environment

This is where the software is developed. This environment should resemble the production environment as much as possible to prevent issues were the software acts differently on production.

Testing Environment / Quality Assurance 1

After the application has been developed to an agreed upon stage it is released to the testing environment. This is where testers (Quality Assurance Engineers provided by the vendor) ensure the quality of the application per the specifications of the design document, create bug reports and review bug fixes are complete as needed. This environment must resemble the production environment accurately, because this is the last safe place to find and fix environment-related bugs.

User Acceptance Test Environment (UAT) / Quality Assurance 2

In a client-vendor projects, the developed software is promoted from internal testing (done by the vendor’s testers) to client testing. This is where the client’s testers verify the quality of the application and send issues for the vendor for repair. This is also where the client assesses the application and can request changes to better fit his requirements within the scope of the design document. This step may not apply to all clients or core code distribution.

Staging Environment / Pre-Production

The staging site is used to assemble, test and review new versions of software before it goes into production. The staging phase of the software life-cycle is often tested on hardware that mirrors hardware used in the production environment. Configuration of the staging site may be different from the development and QA sites, and provides a final QA zone that is separate from the development or production environments. The QA assessment in this step should be quick, but not done in haste and signed-off by all stakeholders before the software is marked to be promoted to production.

Production Environment

This is where the application goes out to the world and become live. Content can be updated in to Production Environment, and new application functionality and bug fixes released from UAT or staging environment can be applied on the next release cycle as development of the software continues. Modifications to the software should never been done in a production environment, except in extreme emergency cases. Access to this host / site is also highly restricted to mitigate untracked modifications.

Required Information

The information that must be provided in the ticket (see procedure below).

  • Username: Current username on the host access is being requested.
  • User Type: Status within the user’s governing group (student developer, employee, etc.).
  • Working Group: The governing group of the user (Research group, department, etc.).
  • Supervisor Contact Information (CC on ticket is sufficient): The contact information for the direct supervisor of the user to be granted access, ultimately responsible for the user’s actions with the granted access.
  • Nature of Access Requested: Description of the type of access requested (ssh access, administrator access, etc.).
  • Role or responsibility of the user, or work to be accomplished with requested access: explain why the access is being requested. Examples: “I manage content”; “I code in PHP and need to work on a component”
    • Does the coder have any training or experience in secure programming?
    • Suggested training: reading "The 2018 Guide to Building Secure PHP Software" https://paragonie.com/blog/2017/12/2018-guide-building-secure-php-software
  • Host-name / Host URL: The identifier of the host where access is requested (dev.hubzero.org, hubzero.org, etc.).
  • Access Time-frame: When is the access needed? When can the access be revoked? (As soon as possible, next week) (Access can be removed at the end of the month, at the end of the semester).
  • For HIPAA-covered hosts, has the user taken the Purdue HIPAA certification?  Has the user encrypted all portable devices (laptop and external drives)?

Policy

Access granted differs by host type and the roles and responsibilities approved by the supervisor, subject to final approval by the appropriate HUBzero staff. Access to production hosts is severely restricted and requires a strong justification. Instead, people should request that changes made elsewhere be copied to production, with a rationale for the change. At no time should any user allow others to use his or her account, or share or fail to secure authentication credentials. Very high privileges (e.g., sudo root access) will require login with an SSH key restricted to an IP address or network, and password login will be disabled. Hubs using NFS for home directories also require storage of the SSH authorized_keys file elsewhere than on the share.

Procedure

  1. User submits support ticket on their governing body’s production host with the required information.
  2. Ticket is processed by the support staff and will wait all for requirements to be collected including supervisor’s approval before proceeding.
  3. Ticket is passed to the appropriate approver on the Hubzero Staff (typically Science Gateway Managers for Administrator access and security officer or system administrator for host access).
  4. Access may be granted within the normal support ticket response cycle.
  5. If access is granted, the ticket is marked as Resolved and closed. The user should test the new access and reopen the ticket if any issues are found.

title: Account Management
content:
See also "Review of Account Privileges" and under Technical Procedures, "Termination Procedures".

System Use Notifications

At login a banner should be displayed on some hubs to state things like "usage may be monitored, recorded, and subject to audit; etc, etc, etc".  The procedure to change this banner is:

  • Login to the administrative interface, a.k.a. backend, at /administrator
  • Navigate to "Menu Manager: Menus"
  • Under "Title", click on "Default"
  • In the list of menu items, under "Title", click on "Login"
  • Enter the banner in the field "Login Description Text"

Password Reset Frequency Limits

The procedure to configure password reset limits is:

  • Consult policy to figure out the number of allowed password resets/hour for the hub in question. 
  • Login to the administrative interface, a.k.a. backend, at /administrator
  • Navigate to Users -> Members -> Options icon (wrench and hammer)
  • In the popup window, go to the tab “Login Settings”
  • Change the “Maximum Reset Count” per time period "Time in Hours" to match

 

Login Failures and Bans

The policy corresponding to this procedure is "Account Management"

The mechanism bans users (i.e., by temporary lockout) that fail more than X logins over an interval of Y hours.  If many users get banned from the same IP address, then that address gets banned by calling fail2ban. 

The duration of individual user bans is up to Y hours, depending on when failed logins "expire" by being outside the time window being considered (the last Y hours).  The duration of the IP bans is set in fail2ban.  There are UI pictures in the regular documentation:

Home › Documentation › 2.1.0 › Internal Docs › Fail2Ban - CMS

which is at fail2ban__cms

This procedure complements that documentation:

  • Consult policy to figure out how banning should be escalated depending on the failure rates
  • Login to the administrative interface, a.k.a. backend, at /administrator
  • Navigate to Users -> Members -> Options icon (wrench and hammer)
  • In the popup window, go to the tab “Login Settings”
  • "Maximum Failed Login Attempts" refers to the number of login failures for an individual account.  The "Time in Hours" determines the rate and the maximum duration of a ban.
  • Select a log retention period to limit the size of the storage, and prevent slower logins when it gets too large.
  • "Fail2ban" refers to the escalation to ban the offending IP address completely, after many user accounts have been banned.  Set it "On", and set the allowed rate of account lockouts that will trigger escalation, per time period in hours.  The "Fail2Ban jail" setting refers to the fail2ban software's internal configuration that will manage those bans.
  • Note that the mechanism ignores login failures from non-existent users.  Don't be alarmed by repeated password-guessing attacks that don't get blocked, if the user doesn't exist.

Login Failures and Bans -- Future Goal

The mechanism first bans (IP, account) pairs.  Continued abuse results in banning the IP address through the fail2ban mechanism.  Continued abuse results in locking the user account, as a last resort. 

This procedure complements that documentation:

  • Consult policy to figure out how banning should be escalated depending on the failure rates
  • Login to the administrative interface, a.k.a. backend, at /administrator
  • Navigate to Users -> Members -> Options icon (wrench and hammer)
  • In the popup window, go to the tab “Login Settings”
  • "Maximum Failed Login Attempts" refers to specific (IP, account) pair login failures.  Also set the "Time in Hours".
  • "Fail2ban" refers to the escalation to ban the offending IP address completely, after many (IP, account) pairs have been banned.  Set in "On", and set the allowed rate of (IP, account) pair blockage that will trigger escalation, per time period in hours.  The "Fail2Ban jail" setting refers to the fail2ban software's internal configuration that will manage those bans.
  • Further login failures for individual accounts eventually result in a lockout or ban of the account.

 

Password Hashing

Passwords are protected from leaks by hashing them. 

  • As above, navigate to Users -> Members -> Options icon (wrench and hammer)
  • In the popup window, go to the tab “Password”
  • Select SHA-512

Password Complexity (Quality) Change Procedure

Password rules are stored in the database table "jos_password_rule";  the UI modifies this table.  They can specify a "character class", e.g., "alpha" for alphabetic characters.  There are already hard-coded character classes (see list below).  If needed, additional ones can be defined in the table "jos_password_character_class".

  • Consult policy to figure out requirements for the hub in question
  • Login to the administrative interface, a.k.a. backend, at /administrator
  • Navigate to Users -> Members -> Passwords
  • Enable the desired rules
  • To change particular values in a rule, click on the rule's description.  For example, the rule "notReused" can have the duration in days, and the description, changed by clicking on the description "Must be different than the previous password (re-use of the same password will not be allowed for one (1) year)"

Example Rule:

minPasswordLength: Passwords must be at least 8 characters long;  set "Value" to 8

List of predefined (hard-coded) character classes ("Class:" input) when creating a password rule:

  • uppercase:  '[A-Z]'
  • numeric: '[0-9]'
  • lowercase: '[a-z]'
  • special: '[!"\'(),-.:;?[`{}#$%&*+<=>@^_|~\]\/\\\]'
  • nonalpha: '[!"\'(),\-.:;?[`{}#$%&*+<=>@^_|~\]\/\\\0-9]'
  • alpha: '[A-Za-z]'

These are defined in the file core/libraries/Hubzero/Password/CharacterClass.php

title: Create a read-only MySQL account
content:
Make sure you read the policy on database accounts before creating accounts.

This procedure has been used on db2.nanohub.org to create a read-only account.  Similar steps can be taken on hubs as well.  Besides being read-only, the privilege grants are designed to prevent reading password hashes.

 

1. Generate a 16-character alphanumeric random password, without special characters

2. Create the account in MySQL

GRANT USAGE ON *.* TO '<username>_ro'@'localhost' identified by '<random password>';

3. Generate an SQL file with the correct grant commands
Enter this multiline command in MySQL, substituting the correct username:

SELECT CONCAT("GRANT SELECT ON nanohub.", table_name, " TO <username>_ro@localhost;")
FROM information_schema.TABLES
WHERE table_schema = "nanohub" AND table_name <> "jos_xprofiles" AND table_name <> "jos_users" AND table_name <> "jos_users" AND table_name <> "jos_users_password" AND table_name <> "jos_users_password_history"  AND table_name <> "jos_xprofiles2" INTO OUTFILE '/var/log/mysql_backups/grants_ro';

4. Load the SQL file into MySQL

grep -v '-' /var/log/mysql_backups/grants_ro | sed 's/|//g' | mysql

5. Additional grant commands
In MySQL, enter the following commands, substituting the correct username:

GRANT SELECT (id, name, username, email, usertype, block, approved, sendEmail,registerDate, lastvisitDate, activation, params, lastResetTime, resetCount) ON nanohub.jos_users TO '<username>_ro'@'localhost';

GRANT SELECT (uidNumber,name , username, email, registerDate, gidNumber, homeDirectory, loginShell, ftpShell, gid, orgtype, organization, countryresident, countryorigin, gender, url, reason, mailPreferenceOption, usageAgreement, modifiedDate, emailConfirmed, regIP, regHost, nativeTribe, phone,proxyUidNumber , givenName, middleName, surname, picture, vip, public, params, note, shadowExpire, locked, orcid) ON nanohub.jos_xprofiles TO '<username>_ro'@'localhost';

flush privileges;

6. Communicate the password to the new user via a secure channel, e.g., write it in a file in the home directory and suggest deleting the file

 

Variant Procedure

This variant procedure solved Ticket #11107 on help.hubzero.org:

Please grant read-only database access on prod communityhub.purdue.edu for usernames "rhine,apsheetz,jgmyers,bmccart,biehl" for tables jos_cart*, jos_storefront*, and jos_users.id, jos_users.name,jos_users.username,jos_users.email, jos_users.lastvisitDate fields only.

We're going to create a new MySQL user account for each, and store the password in /tmp.  Steps to the solution:

  • Create a random password for each new MySQL account
  • Create the MySQL account
  • Grant permissions on the required tables and columns
rand_alnum () {
  openssl rand -base64 15 | sed 's/[^a-zA-Z0-9]//g' | cut -c1-16
}
umask 077
# rhine
for u in  apsheetz jgmyers bmccart biehl; do
  muser=${u}_mysql
  new_pass=`rand_alnum`
  mysql -e "GRANT USAGE ON *.* TO '$muser'@'localhost' identified by '$new_pass'"
  echo "$new_pass" > /tmp/${u}.mysql.pass
  chown ${u} /tmp/${u}.mysql.pass
  for t in `mysql -B --skip-column-names -e "show tables like 'jos_storefront%'" pch`; do
    mysql -e "GRANT SELECT ON pch.$t TO '$muser'@'localhost'"
  done
  for t in `mysql -B --skip-column-names -e "show tables like 'jos_cart%'" pch`; do
     mysql -e "GRANT SELECT ON pch.$t TO '$muser'@'localhost'"
  done
  mysql -e "GRANT SELECT (id, name, username, email, lastvisitDate) ON pch.jos_users TO '$muser'@'localhost'"
  mysql -e "show grants for '$muser'@'localhost'"
done  
mysql -e "flush privileges"

title: Change Management Procedures
content:
Purpose

The purpose of these procedures is to minimize the risk and impact of changes to systems managed by HUBzero and its subcontractors, and make sure related information is shared and communicated appropriately. For purposes of this procedure, a change is defined as anything that transforms, alters, or modifies the operating environment.  For this purpose, the security impacts of changes must be analyzed prior to change implementation.

Definitions

The roles used in this document, and their responsibilities, are described in the HUBzero Incident Response Plan.

Regular Maintenance

No change request is used for scheduled regular routine maintenance, such as patching software, or mandated periodic processes carried on by authorized personel, such as the review of account privileges, which can explicitly result in the revocation of privileges.  That’s because the mandate to perform these tasks is equivalent to approved, standing change requests.

Version Control Repositories

Version control systems, e.g., git, must be used to record changes made to code and Ansible roles and variables, so changes can be re-examined or reversed if any problems are discovered later, and for historical purposes.  Configuration changes to production systems must always be made through Ansible or git code repositories and never directly to the systems with manual changes, to avoid the reversal of manual changes, to make sure that systems can be reconfigured exactly the same way, and to make sure that Ansible and git code repositories are sufficient to describe the state and baseline of all configuration items.  This does not apply to configuration items using the "/administrator" URL of a hub for technical reasons.

Code Changes

All code changes to the "HUBzero CMS", which is stored in the git repository named "hubzero-cms", currently at https://github.com/hubzero/hubzero-cms, are subject to code reviews.  Code reviews are recommended, but not required, for other HUBzero software.

Code reviews must include consideration of the potential security impacts of code changes.  For this purpose, participants in code reviews should include someone trained in secure programming techniques.

CMS Administrator Configuration Changes

Changes to configuration items using the "/administrator" URL of a hub must have been requested by a hub owner, or must be accepted by the hub owners if they will result in changes to the "user experience", defined as system-wide changes visible, or noticeable to users of a HUB by a change of behavior.  For example, changes to password strength and expiration rules must be accepted.  Furthermore, changes to FISMA-certified hubs must be analyzed for potential security impacts by the HUBzero ISO or a designated security analyst.

Changes to or touching security features

After implementation of a change to security features, or a change that touched something used by security features (e.g., a dependency), the related security features shall be tested for correct functionality.  If the change was tracked with a "Trello" card, the card must be labeled "security" and have a checklist added describing the tests to be performed.  Those tests must be completed before the Trello card is moved out of the "In Progress" column.

New Services

Requests for new behaviors and services, etc., MUST be requested via tickets or Trello cards to provide logs and historical records. Change requests via emails, chat, or walk-ins will not be accepted unless a ticket is also filed or a Trello card is created.  When a VIP sends an email requesting changes, the appropriate response for the recipient staff would be to create a ticket or a Trello card on behalf of the VIP, or request a ticket, depending on the situation, assuming the ticketing system is available.

Changes initiated by system administrators MUST be communicated to communication managers if they are likely to or will result in service outages of more than a few seconds.

All changes to FISMA-certified hubs must be analyzed for potential security impacts by the HUBzero ISO or a designated security analyst.

Configuration changes initiated by system administrators that could modify communications received by client browsers or subsystems managed by CMS administrators, MUST be reviewed by CMS administrators before deployment in production. This review will be initiated by a request for review, stating the nature of the change and expected impact, as well as a date by which the review is desired to be done, and a deployment plan. The request can be emailed or transmitted via other means deemed appropriate.  CMS administrators can request discussions in meetings or additional delays for research and testing, as needed, and as circumstances require.

CMS administrators are encouraged to approve security-related changes early for HIPAA-covered hubs, at greater operational risk, due to an increased aversion to security risks. Different outcomes may be desirable for different types of hubs. Communication managers will also be notified at the same time and can veto or delay a change for specific hubs. Communication managers can request additional explanations and meetings with hub stakeholders to discuss the changes.  In all cases, the security impacts of approving, delaying, or rejecting the changes must be taken into account.

Support Requests and Trouble Reports

Inquiries about an error, malfunction or deviations from previously specified behavior SHOULD be reported and resolved via tickets. Reports via emails, chat, or walk-ins will be discouraged, but accepted on a best-effort attempt basis with the expectation that a ticket will be filed. Trivial changes made in response (e.g., tweaking a user’s disk quota) do not need to be logged or communicated. Changes of a greater scale (i.e., systematic changes affecting several HUBs) MUST be communicated if they might result in a noticeable service interruption or in noticeable side effects.

Emergency Work

In case a major problem is detected (e.g., hardware failure, complete outage of a major service), the Incident Response Plan (IRP) should be consulted, with possible escalation to the Disaster Recovery and Business Continuity Plan.  The IRP includes "Communication Guidelines", describing who should communicate what and when.  Additionally, system administrators SHOULD communicate to communication managers that they are aware of a problem and working on it. During emergencies, review processes described in the above sections will not be followed. For this purpose, emergencies are defined as serious threats to the integrity of hubs or to the confidentiality of HIPAA data;  for example, evidence of attempts to compromise a vulnerable service.

title: File Copy Request Between Different Users
content:
Purdue University has an overarching privacy policy and procedure regarding access to departed student files. 

Note the part about "A dean, in the case of an academic unit, a vice president in the case of an administrative unit, and/or a chancellor in the case of a regional campus shall have made a written finding"...  Whenever Purdue faculty staff or students are involved, those should be followed and not what is written below.  If another university or entity is involved, which has specified a policy more restrictive than the one below, that entity's policy should be followed.

DRAFT

This procedure is to be used when a user requests that we make a copy of files owned by a user who is unreachable, e.g., a supervisor wants a copy of a departed student's files.

Required Information

  • Basis justifying the legitimacy of the request, at least one of the following:
    • Explicit student's permission with an explanation of why the student doesn't provide direct access or a copy without our involvement
    • Prior agreement by the student
    • Documented policy of their governing body allowing such copy
  • List of files or directories to copy
  • Destination

Procedure

  1. User submits support ticket on their governing body’s production host with the required information.
  2. A manager of the governing body (hub) approves it
  3. Ticket is processed by the support staff and will wait all for requirements to be collected including manager’s approval before proceeding.
  4. Ticket is passed to a system administrator who will copy the files

Please file a ticket on NanoHUB with the request to have the files restored in Ale's home directory, in a directory name of his choice, and which files or directories he needs.  Please also mention that this conforms with NanoHUB policy (e.g., either the student already accepted this as part of working with Ale, or gave explicit permission later, or such).

title: Review of Account Privileges
content:
The review of account privileges is mandated to happen twice a year for HIPAA compliance.  This procedure was previously kept at https://help.hubzero.org/groups/production/wiki/reviewAccountsPrivs .  This copy supersedes it.

Logs of Actions Taken

During this process, a row will be added to a log whenever privileges are changed, with the date, affected users, affected hub, and description of the action taken (see preparation below).

Preparation

  • Figure out the list of HIPAA-covered hubs
  • Verify the hub assignments of gateway managers
  • Setup log of actions taken
    • Create a wiki page for the year if this is the first review this year, at: https://help.hubzero.org/groups/policies/wiki/account_review_record
    • Setup the table and add an initial row to mark the start of the review

Users Privileged in the CMS (Hub web service)

We need to confirm that the privileges set in /administrator (a.k.a. "backend") are appropriate, for users with greater privileges than "registered".  Ignore the "Worker, HUBzero Solr " user.

For each hub, gather the list of privileged CMS users (see below, "CMS Administrative Backend").  Ask gateway managers to:

  • Create a sub-list minus HUBzero staff;  this is especially useful to remove the names of HUBzero students.  Hub owners should then confirm that the users who have been granted special access and privileges still require them.  
  • Validate that the HUBzero staff with elevated privileges have a legitimate need.  If there's a doubt that the need is sufficient, discuss it, as appropriate, with the staff in question, their manager, the HUBzero ISO and the owner of the hub in question.  Consider saving the results of this discussion for future reference.

Users Privileged in the Operating System

Users can also have elevated privileges in the operating system, allowing "sudo" actions, access to certain files, SSH access, etc...  These are implemented through 2 types of settings.  One type defines roles, and the other defines fine-grained capabilities implemented through group memberships.  In this context, roles are sets of capabilities, so the configuration system converts a role into group memberships. 

Review of the privileges at the OS level will reuse information gathered for the CMS, so it should be done afterwards or concurrently.  If there's any doubt about user privileges for the OS side of things, the verification process defined for the CMS above will be used, but only as necessary for cost containment and efficiency's sake.

List of HIPAA-Covered Machines

For each HIPAA-covered hub, create the list of VMs belonging to it.  Refer to this list in the steps below.

Ansible configuration

Examine in the git repository, the inventory host_vars and group_vars (including the "all" group) for people being granted access, for the roles granted.  The variables of interest is "extra_access_roles:" and "access_roles:".

Local Users

Check for local users with a uid >= 1000;  there shouldn't be any.

Local Groups

Check that membership in the access-* local groups make sense by examining /etc/group.

 

Obsolete, kept for historical puposes

Ogre configuration

Reserve the configuration system ("grab-ogre hostlist").  Examine the Ogre configuration files for "hubname".def, e.g., catalyzecare.org.def and ccehub.org.def, for usernames given a role or access group membership. These will be on lines like:
@define ROLE_XYZ
@define MEMBER_XYZ

Those files are in the directory /usr/share/adm/ogre/private/config/hosts/ . Check also containers such as dev, stage, qa for access. If privileges need to be removed, make sure that access has been removed everywhere, including dev and stage containers, do

grep -r username /usr/share/adm/ogre

Also, except as noted below for individual hosts (e.g., dash.catalyzecare.org), there should not be any user account in /etc/passwd that is above uid 1000. All accounts in /etc/passwd should be recognizable as standard system accounts used for specific services.

On each host, check that groups with elevated privileges through entries in /etc/sudoers, except for the access-* groups checked previously with roles, have appropriate memberships:

glines=`grep ^% /etc/sudoers | awk '{ print $1 }' | grep -v access | sort | uniq`
glinesd=`grep -r ^% /etc/sudoers.d | awk '{ print $1 }' | grep -v access | sort | uniq`
for gl in $glines $glinesd; do
  g=${gl:1}
  getent group  $g
  echo
done

dash.catalyzecare.org

This machine is a special case because it is managed by ITIS-UNIX and Purdue "acmaint" (account management), not by HUBzero's Ogre, and doesn't have a HUB CMS nor uses information from catalyzecare.org. 

The following lists all users with home directories, and their group memberships. The group memberships dictate which information they should have access to. Tunnelers are users that can access MySQL on dash. Check for home directories left over without valid user accounts:

us=`ls /home/users/`
for u in $us; do 
  getent passwd $u > /dev/null
  if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
    echo home directory without valid user account /home/users/$u
  fi
done

us=`ls /home/admin/`
for u in $us; do 
  getent passwd $u > /dev/null
  if [ $? -ne 0 ]; then
    echo home directory without valid user account /home/admin/$u
  fi
done

Check group memberships:
This script isn't saved correctly by the documentation component, as it "eats" characters!  The copy in the old procedures works, at https://help.hubzero.org/groups/production/wiki/reviewAccountsPrivs

SAVEIFS=$IFS
IFS=$(echo -en "backslash n backslash b")
plist=`getent passwd`
for a in ${plist}; do
  id=`echo $a | cut -d ':' -f3`
  uname=`echo $a | cut -d ':' -f1`
  if [ $id -ge 500 ]; then
    groups $uname
  fi
done
IFS=" "

Catalyzecare staff needs to be asked if the above group memberships, and existing user accounts, are correct. Who hasn’t done a login in more than a year?

for u in $us; do 
  times=`last $u -f /var/log/wtmp-* | wc -l`
  # echo $u $times
  if [ $times -lt 3 ]; then
    echo $u not logged in for more than a year
  fi
done

CMS Administrative Backend

  • Login to the /administrator site
  • Navigate to Users -> Members
  • Get the list of users for each available Access Group, except "Public" or "Registered", using the select box that by default shows "Group".  "Registered" users don't have special privileges so we're not interested in reviewing that long list.  
  • Each user requires a justification or approval. Justifications should be commensurate with the powers granted. The number of people in the all-powerful “Super-User” access group should be kept to a minimum, because any compromise of their account is catastrophic. To avoid having too many people as superusers, other access groups should be created to grant a smaller set of privileges.  A user can be a member of several access groups to cover all the needed capabilities.  It's OK for a user to end up having somewhat more capabilities than needed due to the granularity of the access groups.  The number of access groups should remain manageable.
  • The first step is to separate HUBzero staff from other users.  HUBzero staff should be handled internally whenever possible;  do not ask hub owners to validate the entire list. A list of HZ staff would be handy at this step. 
  • Ask hub owners to validate the privileges of users that they manage or that are associated with their organization
  • The position and need of remaining users (not HZ staff, not managed by hub owners) should be clarified, with a default outcome of removing the privileges if they can't be justified
  • DO NOT TRY TO REMOVE ACCESS BY CHECKING THE BOX FOR THEIR NAME AND CLICKING THE "Delete" ICON (near the top right).  You could be deleting the user from the hub.  Instead we want to keep the user but only remove the elevated or unneeded privileges.
  • Remove access by clicking on the user name, which loads a page just for that user.  In the "Assigned Access Groups" area of the user's page, remove the check mark near “SuperUser“ or whichever access group isn't needed. Make sure the user is “Registered” at least.

title: Support Process
content:
Ticket Resolution Process

Support tickets are categorized according to a severity or business impact scale. Hubzero support efforts are prioritized based on the business impact of the issue, and on the support level of the hub, the technology area and/or operating level agreement with third party vendors.

Technical support requests within a severity level are generally processed on a first-come, first-served basis. Critical (severity 1) and High (severity 2) business impact requests that require immediate response or direct help of technical support specialists may be processed out of turn.

When submitting a support ticket, you are requested to supply detailed information (such as name, component, attempted action, expected behavior and observed behavior, steps to reproduce, exact error messages, logs if available, changes made to the system or environment prior to the issue, etc.) for the Hubzero support staff to properly identify and diagnose the issue and speed up response and resolution of the ticket. Failure to supply this information upon request may result in delay of support assistance.

 

Hubzero technical support cannot guarantee a fixed problem resolution period due to a number of influencing factors, amongst them:

  • Customer's timely replies

  • Response time of a third party company

  • The need to prepare and release hotfix, software update, new feature, etc.


The Business Impact / Severity of a support ticket is set according to the guidelines listed below. Since it is not possible to define every possible condition or technical situation, these guidelines can only provide guidance.

 

1 - Critical/System Down (Severity One)

Production application down or major malfunction resulting in a product inoperative condition. Users unable to reasonably perform their normal functions.

 

The specific functionality is mission critical to the business and the situation is considered an emergency.

 

Qualifying Conditions

  • Hub completely unusable

  • Upgrade to a newer version of Hubzero has failed to install.

  • No user can log into the web interface.

 

Support Effort

  • Requires maximum effort from HUBzero and Customer, until an emergency fix is developed or workaround is available.

  • Critical situations may require both Customer and Hubzero personnel to be at their respective work locations on an around-the-clock basis.

  • If the authorized or designated customer contact is not available to engage in this effort, Hubzero Support may reduce the Severity level. If the customer refuses to implement the steps suggested to troubleshoot or correct the issue, Hubzero Support may close the ticket.


 

2 - High (Severity Two)

Critical loss of application functionality or performance resulting in high number of users unable to perform their normal functions. Major feature/product failure; inconvenient workaround or no workaround exists. The program is usable but severely limited.

 

Qualifying Conditions

  • Service interruptions to some, but not all, components (Examples: components not functional for some users but functional for others.)

  • Time sensitive issue reported by Customer, which may adversely affect business impact, monitoring or productivity (Examples: Upcoming conferences, demos and training).

  • In a production system, important tasks cannot be performed, but the error does not impair essential operations (Example: Group approval and Registration Confirmation).

 

Support Effort

  • Requires intensive support effort from Hubzero and Customer, until a fix is developed or workaround is available.

  • Severity 2 situations do not generally require Customer and Hubzero personnel to be at their respective work locations on an around-the-clock basis. Hubzero Support personnel will agree with Customer what effort is required.

  • If the authorized or designated customer contact is not available to engage in this effort, Hubzero Support may reduce the Severity level. If the customer refuses to implement the steps suggested to troubleshoot or correct the issue, Hubzero Support may close the ticket.


 

3 - Normal impact (Severity Three)

Moderate loss of application functionality or performance resulting in multiple users impacted in their normal functions. Minor feature/product failure, convenient workaround exists/minor performance degradation/not impacting production.

 

Qualifying Conditions

  • System is up and running, but the problem causes non-negligible impact. Workaround exists, but it is only temporary (Example: A cron job can be triggered manually but does not run when scheduled.)

  • The software still functions in the Customer's business environment, but there are functional limitations that are not critical in the daily operation (Example: Customer is getting Resources created correctly but wants them to behave in a different manner.)

  • Does not prevent operation of a production system or there is some degradation in performance (Example: The issue affects only users from a specific location.)

  • Moderate loss of application functionality or performance resulting in multiple users impacted in their normal functions (Examples: Some Super Groups experience performance issues due to size and complexity of the group).

  • Important to long-term productivity (Example: Customer cannot set up a particular.)

 

Support Effort

  • Requires moderate support effort from Hubzero and Customer, until a fix is developed or workaround is available.

  • Normal Impact (Severity 3) situations do not require around-the-clock effort.

  • If the customer refuses to implement the steps suggested to troubleshoot or correct the issue, Hubzero Support may close the ticket.

 

4 - Low (Severity Four)

Minor loss of application functionality, product feature requests, how-to questions. The issue consists of "how-to" questions including issues related to one or multiple modules and integration, installation and configuration inquiries, enhancement requests, or documentation questions.

 

Qualifying Conditions

  • Problem does not have significant impact to the Customer or occurs in functionality that is not critical or frequently used (Example: Customer is having trouble with configuration in the Administrative interface).

  • There are no extenuating circumstances that would require this issue to be resolved outside of the normal software. (Example: Customer has general questions about functionality of a particular item. Customer does not understand X in documentation and would like clarification).

  • The problem causes little impact on your operations or a reasonable workaround for the problem has been implemented.

  • The problem results in minimal or no interruptions to normal operations.

  • Non-critical, Minor loss of application functionality or product Feature Request question (Example: Customer wants to know if a particular function is possible).

  • Minor infractions including documentation or cosmetic error not impacting production.

  • Functionality does not match documented specifications.

  • Service enhancements requests.

 

Support Effort

  • Requires low support effort from Hubzero and Customer, until a fix is developed, a workaround is available or an answer to the customer question has been provided.

Low Impact (Severity 4) situations do not require around-the-clock effort.

 

Code Updates

  • Stable Code Updates – Bug fixes in the current supported release.  Updates will be scheduled on a every other week basis and done by Hubzero team.

  • Point Release – Major code updates will be staged first for testing by the hub owner, and scheduled for release into production on a time that is mutually agreed upon.  

  • Code older than the actively supported Hubzero stable versions and/or 3rd party code is the responsibility of the hub and will not be maintained or supported by the HUBzero team.
