title: Account transfer and update from production to dev and stage hosts
content:
People can't register on dev and stage hosts because they share home directories with production.  It would create uid conflicts otherwise, and users on dev could access the home directories of different users on production.  Therefore user accounts need to be transferred from production to dev and stage. 

  1. Run the script: 
    /root/hzbin/transfer_user_acc_to_dev

    on the OpenVZ host where the web server is running.  For example, for catalyzecare.org that is catalyzecare.ogre.hubzero.org.   If you're on the right host then "vzlist" should show something like:

    

catalyzecare:~/hzbin# vzlist
      CTID      NPROC STATUS    IP_ADDR         HOSTNAME
...

     1007        509 running   128.46.22.29    stage.catalyzecare.org
      2000       1088 running   128.46.22.15    dev.catalyzecare.org
      2001       1234 running   128.46.22.14    catalyzecare.org

    However, on Catalyzecare, the production database doesn't have the same name as on dev and stage for a silly reason.  This is the only Hub like this, so instead you need to run transfer_user_acc_to_dev_RUNME, which is the same script but uses the correct database names.

  2. On dev.hubname.org, go to  /administrator/index.php?option=com_system&controller=ldap  and click on the button to export users to LDAP, then export groups to LDAP.
  3. Verify that the OS sees the users with "getent passwd <username>"

title: Ansible HUBzero CMS Update
content:
The repository for the ansible playbook is located on HUBzero's Gitlab System

Prepare the release

  • Update core/bootstrap/version.php
  • Checkout the hubzero-cms repository or pull in the latest changes.
  • Tag the point: v2.1.8-rc1 or v2.1.8, depending on which type of release this is.
git clone https://github.com/hubzero/hubzero-cms
cd hubzero-cms
git checkout 2.1.0
vi core/bootstrap/version.php

If this is the official release we will branch from 2.1.0: git checkout -b 2.1.8

Push the tag and/or branch.

git tag v2.1.8
git push origin v2.1.8

Check the HUBzero Development Group Calendar.

Check to see if there are any major events, such as conferences, classes, or workshops. Are there any entries labeled "Do Not Touch"?

To exclude hubs from the update process, modify the hosts file OR run the playbook with the --limit flag. The following snippet shows the syntax for excluding a hub using the NOT operator (!).

--limit='!notouch.hub.org,!conference.hub.org'

2. Update the Ansible Playbooks

Change the "branch" variable to v2.1.8-rc1 or origin/2.1.8. Branches will need a remote specified.
Commit your changes to this repo, to preserve history.

3. Running the Ansible Playbooks

The playbooks are meant to run in the following order from control.hubzero.org.

ansible-playbook playbooks/update-dev.yml
ansible-playbook playbooks/update-stage.yml
ansible-playbook playbooks/update-courtesy.yml
ansible-playbook playbooks/sync_qa.yml
ansible-playbook playbooks/update-qa.yml
ansible-playbook playbooks/update-production.yml

The Hosts / Inventory File

The hosts file in this repository contains a listing of hubs and their group. To add a new hub, simply add their FQDN to the appropriate group. This should be self-explanatory.


Ansible Vault

Ansible Vault is used to store deployment secrets such as tokens, credentials, or other variables which should not appear in plain-text in the Ansible Playbook.


Permissions and Access

Ansible runs as the hubadmin user on each host. In to run these plays you must


Send your public key to Pascal to add to each hubadmin account's authorized_keys file. (This is currently done by Ogre)
Have Pascal add your account to control.hubzero.org

Additional Readings

The current deployment system is a little daunting to newbies. In the near future it is my goal to simplify the workflow by reducing deployment
to a series of git checkout operations instead of merging of branches and maintaining separate histories for each hub.

Hubzero's Git Flow is outlined here: Link to Hubzero Git Deployment Google Doc  

External contributions will be handled as such: Link to External Contributions Google Doc

title: Git Deployment Workflow
content:
Objective

To reduce the overhead of the CMS deployment via git in HUBzero’s production environment.

Why git?

Git provides a convenient way to track features, bug-fixes, and development history across managed deployments. Git is a decentralized version control system which allows many developers to work on the same codebase, manage conflicting code revisions, and provide a history of changes to document features inline with the code. 

Git is considered an industry standard among developers and since the prevalence of github.com and BitBucket, has become the go-to source code version control system.

Current implementation

Git is currently used a deployment mechanism across all HUBzero-supported production environments. It has worked out well, however has become somewhat cumbersome to administer in its current form. The first problem is that there are two workflows depending on whether the hub’s pipeline has a stage machine or not.

Dev & Prod Pipeline

In the case that a customer’s deployment has a dev and prod configuration only, the customer has their own repository which is a point where their hub’s custom code is merged in with HUBzero’s distribution. This was more profound prior to 2.0.0 Hubzero CMS releases as there was no distinction between customized code and hubzero core code. Since 2.0.0 the hubzero core directory contains code maintained by HUBzero developers and the app directory contains customized code and configurations per hub.
 

< In this setup, the hub’s repository is on the dev.domain.org host usually in the filesystem directory /www/dev. A developer would make changes within /www/dev, commit the changes. The repository would pull from hubzero-cms repository and merge in customizations. When production was to be updated, it would pull from the repository located on the dev host.

The strokes to update the entire pipeline with bleeding edge code would look like:

< Log in as a normal user

ssh user@dev.hub.org


Become a privileged user

sudo su - hubadmin


Get the latest CMS code

git pull


This appeared to rebase local commits on top of hubzero-cms/<version#>-production branch
Fetch was set to https://hubzero.org/git/hubzero-cms.git


Run composer

./muse repository:package install
cd core && ./bin/composer install


Run database migrations

./muse migration -i -f


Fix permissions (for Ogre managed systems)

sudo /usr/share/adm/scripts/check_group_access_php.py

Dev, Stage & Prod Pipeline


The Dev/Stage/Prod pipeline is the general direction we would like to take most deployments. In this configuration, custom code contributions from our clients are introduced on dev which is a clone of the repository hosted on stage. Stage becomes the merge point between hubzero-cms core code and customized code. The production host then pulls from the bare repo (located on stage). 

This configuration’s strokes appear as such:

 

Log in as a normal user

ssh user@dev.hub.org


Become a privileged user

sudo su - hubadmin


Get the latest CMS code

git fetch --all
git merge hubzero-cms 2.1.0-production

This appeared to rebase local commits on top of hubzero-cms/<version#>-production branch
Fetch was set to https://hubzero.org/git/hubzero-cms.git


Run composer

./muse repository:package install
cd core && ./bin/composer install


Run database migrations

./muse migration -i -f


Fix permissions (affects Ogre managed systems)

sudo /usr/share/adm/scripts/check_group_access_php.py

 

Rethinking the Distribution of HUBzero CMS

Separation of the app and core Directories


Releases prior to 1.3.1 the hubzero-cms was distributed as a single directory where customized code was intermixed with “core” code. This means that every production deployment of software was truly it’s own version based on a HUBzero release. Git was relied upon to manage these deployments, keeping track of revisions, merges, and replacement on a per-deployment basis. 

In the past when a customer requested a particular functionality there were two entry points for code through :


The HUBzero Core


The Deployments Dev/Stage Environment

This caused the deployment to become convoluted as each update meant merging the customer’s code with the HUBzero code. 

In HUBzero-CMS version 2.0.0, the distinction of customized code and core code was created. This allows deployment-specific code and configuration to reside apart from the CMS’s core. Idealistically speaking, this allows for the core code to be updated independently of a customer’s special features. The next step would be to create a complementary Git workflow that allows developers (considering third-party developers) to contribute functionality to a specific deployment without breaking the core feature set.

HUBzero Core Git Flow


With the advent of moving to monthly releases it is desired to keep new features out of the “stable” branch. The stable branch is defined as the line of code which currently is installed on production hosts. 

Guideline - All development should be done on the master branch and bug-fixes targeting a specific version should be cherry-picked from master to the version branch.

 

Repository Hosting Scheme


By changing the location and software used to host the repositories required for a HUBzero CMS deployment, the codebase can gain more visibility, contributions, and stability. In this proposed model, “flagship” production-ready code will be presented on github.com for community members to clone and install on their own. 


Sample Development Workflow on an AWS CentOS Box

This is a sample workflow using the HUBzero git repository as a source of code. This is useful for a web development environment and should have some carry overs to any virtual machine, vagrant box, or docker container setup.

Log into the development environment.

ssh centos@<hostname>.aws.hubzero.org

Go to the web root directory.

cd /var/www/

Backup the existing code which will be necessary to preserve the configuration files.

mv hub hub.bak

Clone the development repository, naming it “hub” to preserve the pre-configured location that the web server (Apache) expects.

git clone https://gitlab.aws.hubzero.org/hubzero/hubzero-cms.git hub

Copy the configuration, contained within the app directory, to the new installation.

cp hub.bak/app hub/.

Go to the core directory.

cd hub/core

Pull in external dependencies (including the HUBzero Framework).
 

php composer install

Go back to the /var/www/hub directory and run database migrations.

cd ../
php muse migration -i -f

cd /var/www

Go to the /var/www/ directory

chown apache:apache hub -R

Change the owner and group of the hub directory to something that the web server agrees with.

Chmod 775 hub -R

Change the file mode back to something permissible for development purposes. In production environments this is a little more locked down. 

git pull (--rebase)

Pull the latest code.

Use the rebase command if you already have some commits that you haven’t pushed yet. This puts your work on top of the changes that come downstream.

<make some valid changes to the code>

Fix a bug, for instance.

git add <file>

Add the file(s) to the commit.

git commit -m “[HUB][TICKET#][COM/PLG/MOD/TPL_] Descriptive message”


Form the commit and add a descriptive message meeting the standardized message formatting requirements.


git push


Push your changes upstream.

 

 


Open Merge Request on Gitlab
This starts the code review process. Another developer must approve the code submission(s) before they enter the mainline.
Once approved, an event triggers the change to be pushed into the production branch (located on github.com)


Situation: Deploying a hotfix to Stable/Production deployments
Make the code fix.
Create a commit on the development branches (2.1.0 and master).
Push the commit, so that it may be included in the next release.
Make a patch file.
git format-patch -1 0c0e8b6213d5f5e26fb326ad51fb17db5f5df210 -o ~/patches/.
Upload it to ansible directory.
 ansible-playbook update-production.yml -i hosts -u hubadmin --private-key=~/.ssh/kwojo-hippa-ansible --ask-vault-pass
Run the ansible script (hotfix-prod).


0001-NCIPHUB-1288-PLG_AUTHENTICATION_SHIBBOLETH-Removing-.patch

Place the patch file into the patches directory in the ansible-cms-update repository. 
Situation: Developing a feature targeting a future release
In order to prevent breaking commits from entering an idealistically production-ready

title: Backups
content:
Database Dumps

Backups now finish around 8AM, so can't start them later than they do, 7:30PM.  Databases must be dumped prior to the start of backups, so database dumps must start around 6:30PM.  The use of pigz (parallel gzip) for compressing database dumps minimizes the interval between database dumps and the start of backups.  Without compression, the dumps would use too much disk space and would saturate disk I/O.

Rsync-ZFS

Our ZFS-based backups are run from archive3.hubzero.org and provide a live filesystem to examine and restore from.  They compress on the fly with gzip 9 and store only the differences between versions of files, so they are very efficient.  It runs every night and takes a snapshot after rsyncs.  It also deletes old snapshots, aiming to keep 30 daily snapshots, 12 weekly and 12 monthly images.  This scheme keeps shy of a full year of backups because the current month counts as a monthly image.  The code is published on github.  The ZFS filesystem is replicated to offsite.hubzero.org, hosted at Purdue Calumet in the Powers building.

AWS

We take snapshots and expire them according to policy.

Borg Backups

Borg Backups has been in operation on archive4.hubzero.org since mid-February 2018.  It does compression and deduplication.  It is a "push" system, the opposite of Rsync-ZFS.  The backup server has no access authorization to the clients.  The clients contact the server with dedicated SSH accounts, to access repositories.  The SSH authorized_keys file is used to restrict the actions of clients with a forced command, and the IP addresses that can be used to login.

  • Sudoers can restore files or initiate backups, allowing for delegation and removing system administrators as chokepoints
  • Backup images for a certain date can be mounted as a live filesystem on the client, and used with UNIX utilities to compare and find things
  • Clients compress, deduplicate and encrypt the data, reducing storage and CPU costs on the server.  Each client can choose the compression level
  • ZFS on archive4 provides encryption at rest for Borg Backups, as well as gzip-9 compression. 
    • Ogre-managed clients use the script /usr/share/adm/scripts/borg_run, which by default:
      • Uses zstd-7 compression (Borg Backups v 1.1.4 or higher required).  Use the argument -1 to disable compression, relying on ZFS to provide it.
      • Uses no additional encryption, which allows using compression on the server for weak clients.
    • Clients can use encryption so the server would have no visibility in the backed up files, alleviating concern over the privacy of some personal files.
      • If client encryption is used, keys need to be backed up elsewhere or all is lost if the keys are lost.
  • Backups are easily resumed if interrupted;  Borg Backups creates "checkpoints" at regular intervals, from which backups can be resumed
  • Each client gets its own ZFS filesystem, Borg repository, and own "borg-hostname" account with a restricted SSH key (forced command, etc)
    • This allows backups to operate in parallel and independently, which wouldn't be possible with a single, common repository, because only one client can acces a repo at a time
  • Floating IPs and high-availability setups or shared filesystems have an SSH account separate from the underlying hardware hosts.
    • The NanoHUB fileservers fs6/7 use "borg-fsapps" to backup /apps, /home, /projects, /data
      • There's a possibility of conflict between fs6 and fs7 to access the repo, because typically some partitions are on fs6 and others on fs7;  so they are scheduled at different times
    • The NanoHUB webservers nanohub2 and nanohub3 use "borg-nanohub.org" to backup the ZFS filesystems.  Backups run on the secondary.  There's no conflict possible because only one host is designated as secondary.
    • PURR uses "borg-data.rcac.purdue.edu" to backup PURR projects on Data Depot.  As the borg client can't run on data.rcac.purdue.edu, SSHFS is used to mount that locally at /home/borg/borg-data.rcac.purdue.edu/projects

title: Client changes
content:
Client Name Change

Decide if you want to continue backing up incremental changes or if you want to start fresh. 

  • Continue if the content remained mostly the same, with just a name change and some configuration changes, and you don't need an archive
  • Start fresh by stopping backups for the old name, and doing the procedure for setting up backups for a new host.

To continue, rename the ZFS filesystem for that host on both the West Lafayette campus backup server and the offsite (Calumet) one.  For example:

zfs rename backup/hubzero.org backup/help.hubzero.org
zfs rename offsite/hubzero.org offsite/help.hubzero.org

Then edit the file /etc/zfs-backup/hosts;  comment out or delete the line with the old host's name and add a line with the new one.

Stopping Backups

On the current ZFS-rsync server, edit the file /etc/zfs-backup/hosts and comment out or delete the line with the host's name.  Snapshots will keep getting expired until only the filesystem remains. 

Archiving

See the Fortress section in the old documentation area: https://help.hubzero.org/groups/production/wiki/Fortress

Starting a Backup Manually

Do this to redo a backup that failed, or for the first ever backup.  Run the "zfs-backup" script as root on the ZFS-rsync server, for example:

/usr/share/adm/scripts/zfs-backup qubes.ogre.hubzero.org

title: Restoring MySQL Databases
content:
Decide if you’re restoring from the last dump on the local filesystem, or need to restore from a backup server.  Note that MySQL dumps are scheduled daily around 3:30PM to /var/log/mysql_backups.  You may wish to stop cron temporarily to prevent overwriting yesterday's backup.

Restoring from the last MySQL dump operation

Restoring a single database without disturbing the others:

# Archives were created with pigz but either pigz or gunzip can be used:
pigz -dc /var/log/mysql_backups/<database>.sql.gz  | mysql

# This is an example for removing an obsolete trigger that caused problems:
gunzip -dc /var/log/mysql_backups/<database>.sql.gz  | grep -v 'TRIGGER hg_jos_wiki_version_delete_trigger' | mysql

Changing the Root Password

You may need to do this especially if importing backed up databases, or databases from a different host, fails after loading the new version of the "mysql" database.  Reference: https://www.liberiangeek.net/2014/10/reset-root-password-mariadb-centos-7/

But the reference is missing some important steps at the end;  make sure that mysql is really fully stopped and started again otherwise MySQL will keep running in a vulnerable state.

systemctl stop mariadb.service
service mariadb stop
mysqld_safe --skip-grant-tables --skip-networking &
mysql -u root
use mysql;
flush privileges;
ctrl-D (exit)
myqsladmin shutdown
systemctl stop mariadb.service
# verify that it's really stopped
ps aux | grep mysql
# if needed: pkill mysql
systemctl start mariadb

 

Wipe and Restore:

  1. Erase /var/lib/mysql
  2. Either
    • Generate basic database files allowing MySQL to run by running this as root (on Debian): 
      dpkg-reconfigure mysql-server-5.5

    • Stop MySQL and start it with unrestricted access, similarly to when changing the root password above (example for MariaDB on RHEL 7):

      service mariadb stop
mysqld_safe --skip-grant-tables --skip-networking &
# then restore the tables as per the next step.
# Make sure to fully stop it after the restore to restrict access again!
  3. To restore from the files in /var/log/mysql_backups: 
    cd /var/log/mysql_backups
for d in `ls *.sql.gz`; do
   echo $d
   gunzip -dc $d | grep -v 'TRIGGER hg_jos_wiki_version_delete_trigger' | mysql
done
/etc/init.d/mysql restart

Restoring from ZFS backups

  1. Figure out which snapshot to restore from. For example, this will select the snapshot of 1 day ago on archive3.hubzero.org: 
    days_ago=1
victim=<your hostname>
victim_snapshot=`ls /backup/$victim/.zfs/snapshot | tail -n $days_ago | head -n 1`
echo snapshot to be used: $victim_snapshot

    For NanoHUB, check /backup/nanohub.org/.zfs/snapshot/ regardless of which host is active.

  2. Transfer the files in /var/log/mysql_backups back to the host. For NanoHUB, use /varshared/log/mysql_backups
    Example:  
    # ls /backup/$victim/.zfs/snapshot/$victim_snapshot/var/log/mysql_backups/
mysql.sql.gz  pch.sql.gz  pch_metrics.sql.gz  prj_db_4.sql.gz
scp /backup/$victim/.zfs/snapshot/$victim_snapshot/var/log/mysql_backups/ $victim:/root/tmp/
  3. Continue with the instructions to restore from the local filesystem, as above.

Restore specific tables on nanoHUB:

Find out which database the table is in.  Then grep the INSERT statements out of the MySQL dump.  ESCAPE THE BACKTICKS, backslashes are deleted by the documentation module.  For example, tables selected with a wild card:

ls /backup/nanohub.org/.zfs/snapshot/
date=2017-08-15.23-23-21
cd /backup/nanohub.org/.zfs/snapshot/$date/varshared/log/mysql_backups
# watch out for missing backslashes that are removed by the documentation module
zgrep "INSERT INTO `jos_citation.*`" nanohub.sql.gz > /root/nano_$date
ls /root/nano_$date
vi /root/nano_$date

scp /root/nano_* nanohub.org:/home/nanohub/kwojo314/

on NanoHUB:
chown kwojo314 /home/nanohub/kwojo314/nano_*

Another example for specific tables:

table=jos_users
echo "DELETE FROM  `$table`;" > /root/nano_${table}_${date}
zgrep "^INSERT INTO `$table`" /backup/nanohub.org/.zfs/snapshot/$date/varshared/log/mysql_backups/nanohub.sql.gz >> /root/nano_${table}_${date}
table=jos_xprofiles
echo "DELETE FROM  `$table`;" > /root/nano_${table}_${date}
zgrep "^INSERT INTO `$table`" /backup/nanohub.org/.zfs/snapshot/$date/varshared/log/mysql_backups/nanohub.sql.gz >> /root/nano_${table}_${date}
table=jos_auth_link
echo "DELETE FROM  `$table`;" > /root/nano_${table}_${date}
zgrep "^INSERT INTO `$table`" /backup/nanohub.org/.zfs/snapshot/$date/varshared/log/mysql_backups/nanohub.sql.gz >> /root/nano_${table}_${date}

 

Extract the user tables while erasing the password hashes

cd /backup/habricentral.org/.zfs/snapshot/2017-04-02.02-00-17/var/log/mysql_backups/
zgrep "INSERT INTO `jos_users`" habricentral.sql.gz | sed -e "s/{[A-Z]*}[^']*//g" > /root/habri_April

Extract table creation statements: -A option includes a number of lines after the match

cd /backup/habricentral.org/.zfs/snapshot/2017-07-11.22-09-29/var/log/mysql_backups/
zgrep -A 5 "CREATE TABLE `jos_users`" habricentral.sql.gz

title: Restoring Borg Backups
content:
Borg Backups uses a repository for each host, and an archive (that means a successful backup) for each partition and date.  Restores can be done in these manners:

  • Initiated from the client, restoring specific directories, files, or an entire partition
  • Restoring an entire host is done by restoring each filesystem one at a time (filesystems are backed up one by one)
  • Specific archives can be mounted on the server, archive4
  • Specific archives can be mounted on the client

Exception: PURR Data Depot Backups

The descriptions below do not directly apply to PURR's Data Depot storage.  Those backups are done directly on archive4, by user "borg-data.rcac.purdue.edu", from an SSHFS mount of Data Depot.  Equivalents to the scripts described below are in that user's home directory. Otherwise the same instructions apply.

List Backup Archives

Use the script /usr/share/adm/scripts/borg_client_list to make your life easier.  It will print a list of all images for each partition, followed by repository information, and an explanation of the names of the backups.  Note that the argument is the hostname of the backup server, not the client.  For example:

# /usr/share/adm/scripts/borg_client_list archive4.hubzero.org

Available backup archives:
-2018-02-28.19-30-03                 Wed, 2018-02-28 19:30:05 [83befb49232bf3002609668d3299f63dbc775d92abcf718aa29c1bd94050b37b]
-2018-03-31.19-30-04                 Sat, 2018-03-31 19:30:08 [a89a0160968a39e6cfab096b7b66676b3743c5dc374248908b567da99dc9465c]
-2018-04-15.19-30-03                 Sun, 2018-04-15 19:30:05 [4ea04a38b32c4dca4d4b90664c84ddb74bb6b382427eeb6e8875992250c67d08]
-2018-04-22.19-30-04                 Sun, 2018-04-22 19:30:05 [a61c53bcfa54e621b2206e47f24b5b6fbdde9faf2f4754ee6380de522e3292e6]
-2018-04-29.19-30-07                 Sun, 2018-04-29 19:30:15 [4f7c71ae58f083ad54e3ce3a7d44b4c5949839308b6787f7ea2ac4ec57f83c90]

...

Partitions are backed up as follows:
/ backed up as -date

Restore Files with /usr/share/adm/scripts/borg_client_restore

On the client, figure out which archive you want to use (see above).  Important:  cd into the directory where you want the restored files to go.  If you don't want to overwrite things, create a new directory for the restore, and cd into it.  Then run the script, for example:

/usr/share/adm/scripts/borg_client_restore archive4.hubzero.org db-2018-09-13.03-06-28 re:db/dev/deeds/submit/sessions/.*/[0-9]*/output/submit.finish

where the last argument is a pattern recognized by Borg.  A prefix tells Borg which kind of pattern it is, e.g., "sh:", "re:" or "pp:".  If you don't use a prefix, you may be surprised by the files you do or don't get.  You don't need a prefix if you just specify the path to a directory.

You may wish to edit the script first, and add options like "--list" or "--dry-run" to the borg extract command.

WARNING: if you restore specific files only, directories above those files may be restored with root:root ownerships and default permissions instead of the original ones.

Restore Files with Borg Extract

The steps are:

  • Setup the environment for the commands
    • Borg environment variables are useful
    • "LANG=en_US.UTF-8" may be needed
  • Run "borg list" to figure out the name of the archive you want to restore from.  Note that the time and date are when the backup STARTED, not when it finished, whereas rsync backup snapshots have the time when it finished
  • Change directories to where you want files restored
    • Note that the whole directory hierarchy is recreated, e.g., restoring /var/log/audit in place results in /var/log/audit/var/log/audit.  A "mv" or "cp" operation is then needed to complete the restore.
    • Extraneous files are not removed
  • Run "borg extract --numeric-owner /path/to/repo::filesystem-date /path/to/directory" to restore a directory from the backup done on a certain date

Example 1, restore a single file:

# setup environment so the commands use SSH with the correct private key
borg_server=archive4.hubzero.org
hostname=`hostname -f`
BORG_RSH="ssh -i /usr/share/adm/ogre/secret/hosts/$hostname/borg_$hostname"
export BORG_RSH
BORG_REPO=ssh://borg-$hostname@$borg_server/repo
export BORG_REPO

# figure out which archive you want 
borg list borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo

# This fails because the path must not include the mount point:

devsubmit-64:~# borg extract --numeric-owner borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo::-2018-05-05.00-11-06 /opt/submit/SubmitCommand.py
Include pattern '/opt/submit/SubmitCommand.py' never matched.

# This works because "/" (the mount point) was removed from the path to the wanted file:

devsubmit-64:~# borg extract --numeric-owner borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo::-2018-05-05.00-11-06 opt/submit/SubmitCommand.py
devsubmit-64:~# ll /root/opt/submit/
total 72K
drwx------ 2 root    root 4.0K May 19 06:47 .
drwx------ 3 root    root 4.0K May 19 06:47 ..
-rw-r----- 1 clarksm apps  60K Apr 30 11:52 SubmitCommand.py
devsubmit-64:~#

Example 2 (more automation, appropriate for restoring an OpenVZ container from within):

# setup environment so the commands use SSH with the correct private key
borg_server=archive4.hubzero.org
hostname=`hostname -f`
BORG_RSH="ssh -i /usr/share/adm/ogre/secret/hosts/$hostname/borg_$hostname"
export BORG_RSH
BORG_REPO=ssh://borg-$hostname@$borg_server/repo
export BORG_REPO

partition=/
# cd $partition 
date=2018-02-28
LANG=en_US.UTF-8
sp=`echo ${partition#/} | tr '/' '_'`
archive_name=`borg list borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo | grep -- ^$sp-$date | cut -f1 -d ' '`
echo restoring $archive_name
time borg extract borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo::$archive_name


Example 3: restore all partitions, e.g., on an OpenVZ host

date=2018-02-28
plist=`grep -e xfs -e ext[2-4] /etc/fstab | grep -v -e '^#' -e /mnt/db-raid |  awk '{ print $2 }'`
for partition in $plist; do
  case $partition in

  "/var/lib/vz")
    # OpenVZ: backup only templates
    # backup running containers from the inside
    partition="/var/lib/vz/template"
    ;;
    
  "/vz")
    partition="/vz/template"
    ;;

  # don't backup KVM raw files, backup the image from the inside of the VM
  "/var/lib/libvirt/images")
    continue
    ;;

  # don't backup raw database partitions, instead backup the logical dumps
  "/var/lib/mysql"*)
    continue
    ;;

  "/export/mysql")
    continue
    ;;

  "/var/lib/postgresql")
    continue
    ;;

  # don't backup temporary MySQL table scratch space
  "/var/mysqltmp")
    continue
    ;;

  "/tmp")
    continue
    ;;

  # Don't backup Pegasus scratch space
  "/pegtmp")
    continue
    ;;

  # don't backup the Debian repo mirrors
  "/var/spool/apt-mirror")
    continue
    ;;
  esac
  sp=`echo ${partition#/} | tr '/' '_'`
  archive_name=`borg list borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo | grep -- ^$sp-$date | cut -f1 -d ' '`
  echo restoring $archive_name
  cd $partition 
  time borg extract borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo::$archive_name
  echo you still need to move or copy the restored files at $partition/$partition
done

Example 4: Floating IPs (NanoHUB home, apps)

Floating IPs are backed up by the script /usr/share/adm/scripts/borg_run_floating

 

# setup environment so the commands use SSH with the correct private key
hostname=`cat /etc/borg/float.repo`
borg_server=archive4.hubzero.org
usernamelong=borg-$hostname
username=${usernamelong:0:32}
# BatchMode sets ServerAliveInterval to 300 and ServerAliveCountMax to 3, so use "borg --lock-wait 1000"
BORG_RSH="ssh -i /usr/share/adm/ogre/secret/hosts/$hostname/borg_$hostname -o BatchMode=yes"
export BORG_RSH
BORG_REPO=ssh://$username@$borg_server/repo
export BORG_REPO

TEMP=/root/tmp
export TEMP
mkdir -p /root/tmp

# figure out which partition you want to restore
cat /etc/borg/floats
partition=/export/home
sp=`echo ${partition#/} | tr '/' '_'`

# figure out which archive you want
borg list $username@$borg_server:repo

cd /root/tmp
borg extract --numeric-owner $username@$borg_server:repo::export_home-2018-05-21.20-12-05 export/home/nanohub/mmh/notebooks
mv export/home/nanohub/mmh/notebooks /export/home/nanohub/mmh/notebooks

 

  

Borg Mount

For OpenVZ containers look below.

"borg mount" can be very useful to verify a backup, by doing something like "diff -qr" or "rsync --dry-run".  Similarly to the above:

  • Check that "fuse" can be used -- this may not work inside some OpenVZ containers
  • Setup the environment for the commands
  • Run "borg list" to figure out the name of the archive you want to restore from
  • Change directories to where you want files restored
  • Run "borg mount"

Example:

LANG=en_US.UTF-8
mkdir /mnt/borg
borg mount -o ro borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo::(archive name) /mnt/borg

Example 2: Mount archives for all partitions under /mnt/borg-(partition)

Select the date below and the archives from that date will be used:

date=2018-02-28 

for m in `ls -d /mnt/borg*`; do
  echo $m
  umount $m
done 

rmdir /mnt/*

# setup environment so the commands use SSH with the correct private key
borg_server=archive4.hubzero.org
hostname=`hostname -f`
BORG_RSH="ssh -i /usr/share/adm/ogre/secret/hosts/$hostname/borg_$hostname"
export BORG_RSH
BORG_REPO=ssh://borg-$hostname@$borg_server/repo
export BORG_REPO

plist=`grep -e xfs -e ext[2-4] /etc/fstab | grep -v -e '^#' -e /mnt/db-raid |  awk '{ print $2 }'`
for partition in $plist; do
  case $partition in

  "/var/lib/vz")
    # OpenVZ: backup only templates
    # backup running containers from the inside
    partition="/var/lib/vz/template"
    ;;
    
  "/vz")
    partition="/vz/template"
    ;;

  # don't backup KVM raw files, backup the image from the inside of the VM
  "/var/lib/libvirt/images")
    continue
    ;;

  # don't backup raw database partitions, instead backup the logical dumps
  "/var/lib/mysql"*)
    continue
    ;;

  "/export/mysql")
    continue
    ;;

  "/var/lib/postgresql")
    continue
    ;;

  # don't backup temporary MySQL table scratch space
  "/var/mysqltmp")
    continue
    ;;

  "/tmp")
    continue
    ;;

  # Don't backup Pegasus scratch space
  "/pegtmp")
    continue
    ;;

  # don't backup the Debian repo mirrors
  "/var/spool/apt-mirror")
    continue
    ;;
  esac

  sp=`echo ${partition#/} | tr '/' '_'`
  mkdir -p /mnt/borg-$sp
  # archive_name=$sp-$date
  archive_name=`borg list borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo | grep -- ^$sp-$date | cut -f1 -d ' '`
  echo borg mount -o ro borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo::$archive_name /mnt/borg-$sp
done

# Use the mount points to do an rsync (10x slower than borg extract) or whatever else you need

for m in `ls -d /mnt/borg*`; do
  echo $m
  p=`echo /${m#/mnt/borg-} |  tr '_' '/'`
  time rsync -vcax --dry-run $p/ $m$p/ | grep -v -e puppet -e ^tmp -e /tars/ -e ^run -e root/.cache/borg/ -e ^var/lib/apt/ -e var/cache/ -e var/backups/ -e var/log/letsencrypt/ -e sftp/ -e var/lib/dpkg -e var/lib/spamassassin/
  echo
done

Example 3: Borg Mount and OpenVZ containers: not recommended

Unless the container has access to fuse, the mount will have to be done on the underlying OpenVZ host. This complicates things.

# somehow when run in a terminal as root, it's different than from this script?
export BORG_UNKNOWN_UNENCRYPTED_REPO_ACCESS_IS_OK=yes
# on archive4, invoking borg locally sets this off when it's run from cron later
export BORG_RELOCATED_REPO_ACCESS_IS_OK=yes

# Does archive4 allow connections from the OpenVZ server?
vzlist
hostname=labs.catalyzecare.org
ctid=2010
ll /vz/private/$ctid/usr/share/adm/ogre/secret/hosts/$hostname/borg_$hostname

# Allow access to the repository on archive4 from the OpenVZ host (normally access is only from the container):
hostname=labs.catalyzecare.org
cat /home/borg/borg-$hostname/.ssh/authorized_keys
vi .ssh/authorized_keys

# Back on the OpenVZ server:
BORG_RSH="ssh -i /vz/private/$ctid/usr/share/adm/ogre/secret/hosts/$hostname/borg_$hostname"

borg list borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo
archive_name=
LANG=en_US.UTF-8
borg mount -o ro borg-$hostname@$borg_server:repo::$archive_name /mnt/borg

# verify without checksums (very fast)
rsync -vcax --dry-run /vz/private/$ctid/ /mnt/borg/ | grep -v -e ^tmp -e ^run -e root/.cache/borg/ -e ^var/lib/apt/ -e var/cache/ -e var/backups/ -e var/log/letsencrypt/ 

# verify with checksums (-c option): slow but thorough, this is effectively a complete restore operation
rsync -vcax --dry-run /vz/private/$ctid/ /mnt/borg/ | grep -v -e ^tmp -e ^run -e root/.cache/borg/ -e ^var/lib/apt/ -e var/cache/ -e var/backups/ -e var/log/letsencrypt/

title: Restoring Riak from Backups
content:
Using Rsync-ZFS backups

 

-- Riak is out of service on catalyzecare.org as of June 2018, solr is used instead --

A dedicated ZFS filesystem is used for Riak, separate from the host.  See the script used for backups, /usr/share/adm/scripts/zfs-backup-riak.  The backups are binary backups so the riak service must be stopped completely before restore, and started again after.

WARNING:  "service riak start/stop" does something different from "riak start" and "riak stop", or at least systemd is confused after using "riak stop".

ssh archive3
cd /backup/db.catalyzecare.org.riak

ssh db.catalyzecare.org 'riak stop'
ssh db.catalyzecare.org 'riak ping'
rsync -ax --numeric-ids var/lib/riak/ db.catalyzecare.org:/var/lib/riak/
rsync -ax --numeric-ids etc/riak/ db.catalyzecare.org:/etc/riak/
ssh db.catalyzecare.org 'riak start'
ssh db.catalyzecare.org 'riak ping'

title: Restoring SOLR
content:
This is about SOLR as used on catalyzecare.org, not the SOLR instances used by the CMS to support search.  Backups are done by making SOLR create snapshots just before the backup systems run.  The snapshots are then used for restores.

See https://gitlab.hubzero.org/junkda/solr-backup-restore for the most up to date information and scripts.

SOLR Snapshot command (will keep 5 days of snapshots)

wget -q -O - http://localhost:8983/solr/mappings/replication?command=backup&numberToKeep=5&location=/opt/solr/backups/mappings
wget -q -O - http://localhost:8983/solr/actlog/replication?command=backup&numberToKeep=5&location=/opt/solr/backups/actlog
wget -q -O - http://localhost:8983/solr/dla/replication?command=backup&numberToKeep=5&location=/opt/solr/backups/dla
wget -q -O - http://localhost:8983/solr/dlc/replication?command=backup&numberToKeep=5&location=/opt/solr/backups/dlc
wget -q -O - http://localhost:8983/solr/files/replication?command=backup&numberToKeep=5&location=/opt/solr/backups/files
wget -q -O - http://localhost:8983/solr/uploads/replication?command=backup&numberToKeep=5&location=/opt/solr/backups/uploads
wget -q -O - http://localhost:8983/solr/mon/replication?command=backup&numberToKeep=5&location=/opt/solr/backups/mon

Snapshotting the DLA core takes a long time. Preferably, we should be issuing the snapshot command an hour or so before running the file system backup. See the README in the referenced gitlab repo for more information.

Restoration requires 4 steps: https://gitlab.hubzero.org/junkda/solr-backup-restore#restoration-information has the most up to date information.

A brief summary:

1. Verify SOLR configuration

2. Create SOLR cores.

3. Create Schema for each core.

4. Issue the core restoration command.

 

Depending on the nature of the failure, one or more of the above 4 steps may be skipped.

Rsync-ZFS Backups

  1. Define new client

    Example:
    hostname=hubzero.org
  2. On control.hubzero.org, prepare to change the host configurations in Ogre:
    grab-ogre  director  ${hostname}
  3. Add "zfs-client" and "bacula_filed" to SET_CLASSES in ${hostname}.def
  4. Update the configuration of ${hostname}:
    iro <hostname>
  5. Login on archive3.hubzero.org
  6. vi /etc/zfs-backup/hosts and add the host(s) to the list, one host per line, in the order they are to be backed up.
  7. If only certain partitions are to be backed up, e.g., for a floating IP, create a ${hostname}.parts file in /etc/zfs-backup.  One line per partition to be backed up.
  8. Verify that the client is reachable via SSH and accept the host's key:
    ssh ${hostname}
  9. For Bacula backups, run /root/pascal/makehub2/bacula_add ${hostname}

  11. Figure out the least used  "Fullx" schedule, where x is from 0 to 12, using the commands in the comments at the beginning of the director.hubzero.org.def file

  1. On control.hubzero.org, run "/usr/share/adm/scripts/borg_setup_control hostname archive4.hubzero.org".  It will create an SSH key pair and distribute it.
  2. On archive4.hubzero.org, run "/usr/share/adm/scripts/borg_setup_server hostname [extra_IPs]".  It will create a dedicated user, a ZFS filesystem, and an authorized_keys file with the appropriate "from" option.  The optional extra_IPs are comma separated IP addresses that are allowed to access the account and are added to the "from" option.
  3. On the client, run /usr/share/adm/scripts/borg_run archive4.hubzero.org [compression_level]", where the compression level should be no higher than 3 and applies to "zstd" compression (BB v 1.1.4 required).  A value of "1" is much faster than "3" but with less compression.  A value of "-1" disables compression, instead relying on the backup server to compress.  This script also does pruning after a backup.

  4. If you run backups differently take note:  if you use encryption on the client, you must use compression on the client as well, at least lz4, which is very light weight.  The server cannot compress encrypted backups, and backups without any compression will be very expensive.

title: Archiving to Fortress
content:
Previous versions of this document at: https://help.hubzero.org/groups/production/wiki/Fortress

The general idea is to

  • compress and encrypt the last backup of a host
    • Use gpg with the archival public key
    • 7zip for compression because we pay the compression cost once but the storage cost is forever
  • send it to Fortress
    • Need to use their security tokens
    • Need to use the hsi software provided by package "hsi-htar" from rcac software repository, e.g.,  http://hpss.rcac.purdue.edu/yum-public/rcac_rhel7-public-$basearch/RPMS.rcac_public (see Fortress documentation)
  • Verify that the archive is complete by decrypting, decompressing and comparing with last backup
  • Verify that it copied correctly to Fortress by creating hashes and comparing them
    • Need the passphrase for the private key

Fortress info:

http://www.rcac.purdue.edu/userinfo/resources/fortress/

Our HUBzero space on Fortress is in /group/hubzero and is group setuid. New administrators for hubzero simply need an account on RCAC systems and to be added to the “hubzero” group:

drwxrwsr-x 2 pmeunier hubzero 512 Sep 6 14:28 .

To communicate with Fortress, you need a token. To (re)generate a token, do:

ssh pmeunier@data.rcac.purdue.edu 
/opt/hsi/bin/hsi

Transfer the token to the backup host:

scp pmeunier@data.rcac.purdue.edu:.private/hpss.keytab .private/hpss.keytab

List of Host Backups to Fortress

On a ZFS backup server, find those that have the fewest snapshots and are not backed up anymore:

cd /backup
for host in `ls`; do   echo `zfs list -H -t snapshot -r backup/$host | wc -l` $host; done | grep -v ARCHIVE | sort -n | head

Instructions to archive a retired host:

screen bash
cd /backup 
host= (type FQDN)

we will archive only the filesystem without the snapshots:

zfs list -t snapshot -r backup/$host
for b in `zfs list -H -t snapshot -r backup/$host | cut -f 1`; do echo $b; zfs destroy $b; done

Create the archive with 7zip compression, with “nice” priority (10) so backups can still run:

nice tar -c -p --to-stdout $host | nice 7za a -an -txz -so -si | nice gpg --recipient  "Pascal Meunier 2016 archiving key (4096 bits) <pmeunier@purdue.edu>" -e -z0 -o /backup/ARCHIVE/$host.tar.7z.gpg

Previously we used the gpg -z9 option but 7zip is much better (although slower). As an example, with 7zip an archive was 799M vs 1.2G using -z9. For the record this is the old command:

tar -c -p --to-stdout $host | gpg --recipient  "Pascal Meunier 2016 archiving key (4096 bits) <pmeunier@purdue.edu>"  -e -z9 -o /backup/ARCHIVE/$host.tar.gpg

It’s important to verify that the archive is complete; the process could have stopped early. Verify, and upload it to Fortress:

nice gpg --decrypt /backup/ARCHIVE/$host.tar.7z.gpg | nice 7za e -an -txz -so -si | nice tar --compare -C /backup

Upload to Fortress:

cd /backup/ARCHIVE/
/opt/hsi/bin/hsi -h fortress.rcac.purdue.edu -l pmeunier "cd /group/hubzero; umask 017; put $host.tar.7z.gpg; chmod g+rw $host.tar.7z.gpg"
/opt/hsi/bin/hsi -h fortress.rcac.purdue.edu -l pmeunier "ls -al /group/hubzero"

Calculate MD5 hashes to verify integrity:

md5sum  $host.tar.7z.gpg > $host.tar.7z.gpg.md5
cat $host.tar.7z.gpg.md5
/opt/hsi/bin/hsi -h fortress.rcac.purdue.edu -l pmeunier "cd /group/hubzero; hashcreate $host.tar.7z.gpg"
/opt/hsi/bin/hsi -h fortress.rcac.purdue.edu -l pmeunier "cd /group/hubzero; hashls $host.tar.7z.gpg"

and compare the hashes. If they match we can delete the copy on archive3:

rm  /backup/ARCHIVE/$host.tar.7z.gpg

To remove the archived backups:

/usr/share/adm/scripts/dirvish-delete $host
rm -rf /backup/ARCHIVE/$host
zfs destroy backup/$host
zfs destroy offsite/$host

and make sure the host’s name is removed from /etc/zfs-backup/hosts

To check stored archives and retrieve them

/opt/hsi/bin/hsi -h fortress.rcac.purdue.edu -l pmeunier
cd /group/hubzero
ls -al
get alt.nanohub.org.tar.gpg

To decrypt:

/opt/hsi/bin/hsi -h fortress.rcac.purdue.edu -l pmeunier "cd /group/hubzero; get $host.tar.gpg"
gpg --decrypt $host.tar.gpg | tar -xv $host.backup
(enter passphrase;  hint: an important event)

Note that there is no requirement to use the user “pmeunier”, it just needs to be a user in the group “hubzero”.

total 340K
